additionalTests.name: testTerminalSyncStateSurvivesRelaunchAndIsClearedOnlyByAnAcceptedWrite
additionalTests.pins: Durability and lifecycle of terminalSyncFailureIDs, which round 4 introduced as durable state but no test restores from UserDefaults. It also pins that syncFailureReasons is session-scoped (empty after relaunch) so ShareDropSheet's fallback copy is the one that actually ships, and that a terminal id is retired the moment a fresh write is accepted (enqueueCloudSync -> clearTerminal -> ack) rather than lingering as a permanent orange banner. Currently nothing covers the restore path at DropStore.swift:259-260 or the clearTerminal call at :442, and nothing checks that terminal ids for drops that no longer exist are ever reaped.
additionalTests.steps: ARRANGE: defaults = makeDefaults(); cloud = GatedCloudStore(); library = makeLibrary(cloud: cloud, defaults: defaults); let drop = GeoDrop(); await cloud.setFailSave(DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount, for: drop.id); try await library.add(drop); try await waitUntil { library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) }. ACT/ASSERT 1 (relaunch): let library2 = DropLibrary(localStore: sameLocalStore, cloudStore: cloud, defaults: defaults); XCTAssertTrue(library2.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id)); XCTAssertNil(library2.syncFailureReasons[drop.id], "the detail text does not survive — the fallback copy is what ships"). ACT/ASSERT 2 (recovery): await cloud.setFailSave(nil, for: drop.id); try await library2.update(drop, persist: true); try await waitUntil { !library2.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) }; XCTAssertEqual(defaults.stringArray(forKey: "terminalSyncDropIDs") ?? [], [], "the durable set must be cleared on disk, not just in memory"). ACT/ASSERT 3 (phantom ids): mark a second drop terminal, delete its row out from under the library (simulate a quarantine wipe by emptying the local store file directly), await library2.refresh(near: nil), and assert the terminal banner count does not still claim a drop that no longer exists.
additionalTests.infrastructure: GatedCloudStore needs setFailSave(_:for:) to accept nil to clear a per-id failure. A shared LocalDropStore URL so two DropLibrary instances model a relaunch over one file plus one defaults suite. No new doubles otherwise.

additionalTests.name: testCloudDeleteOfANeverUploadedDocumentIsSatisfiedRatherThanRefused
additionalTests.pins: The round-4 error mapping at FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-95 — the ONE place that decides whether a tombstone is retired or kept forever — is completely untested, and the stated platform rules produce permission-denied (resource == null), not notFound, for exactly the case the mapping was written for. This test pins the mapping against the error the rules actually emit, and pins that the seam never swallows a genuine refusal (an owner-mismatch delete must still propagate).
additionalTests.steps: ARRANGE: introduce a DocumentDeleting seam (protocol with `func delete(_ path: String) async throws`) that FirebaseDropStore calls instead of Firestore directly, and an actor double scripted per path. CASE 1: script the double to throw NSError(domain: FirestoreErrorDomain, code: FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied.rawValue) for a drop whose ownerUid is nil (never uploaded); ACT: try await store.delete(drop); ASSERT: no error thrown, "a delete of a document that cannot exist is satisfied, not refused". CASE 2: same error code but for a drop whose ownerUid is another uid; ASSERT: the call still short-circuits at the existing ownership backstop and issues no network delete (await double.calls == 0). CASE 3: script a genuine NSError(code: FirestoreErrorCode.unavailable.rawValue); ASSERT: XCTAssertThrowsError, "a transient refusal must still propagate so the tombstone is retried". CASE 4 (library level): with the mapping in place, add + remove a never-acked drop against a GatedCloudStore whose delete throws permission-denied, and assert library.pendingDeleteIDs is empty afterwards — the Profile "Synced" precondition is restored.
additionalTests.infrastructure: New DocumentDeleting protocol + injectable dependency on FirebaseDropStore (it currently reaches for Firestore.firestore() inline, which is why this path has no coverage at all), and an actor recording double scripted with per-path errors. Case 4 reuses GatedCloudStore and the injected UserDefaults suite.

soundAreas: FirestoreAcked (Services/FirestoreAcked.swift:16-34) is a correct single seam: the throwing continuation is resumed exactly once on every path, the synchronous encode failure is resumed explicitly (the completion genuinely never fires there), and all three callers — FirebaseDropStore.save (FirebaseDropStore.swift:74), AccountService seeding/edit, ReactionService.send (ReactionService.swift:46) — now route through it. No raw setData survives outside that file.

The write-pipeline generation discipline is now complete and correctly ordered: entry check before issuing the write (DropStore.swift:455), a re-check after the save await before every bookkeeping mutation (461, 470, 475), and a defer that only nils syncTasks for the owning generation (456-458). The gated-interleaving test (testSupersededSyncTaskCannotClearPendingWhenItFinallyResumes) parks a task exactly where production parks offline and genuinely pins it.

Terminal-failure precedence is implemented consistently across all three surfaces and outranks the reassuring caption in each: ProfileScreen.swift:78-87 (before lastSyncError, pending and Synced), DropsListScreen.swift:39-47, ShareDropSheet.swift:135-143. clearTerminal is correctly invoked on remove() (DropStore.swift:383) and on a fresh user-initiated write (442), and the durable set survives relaunch via terminalDefaultsKey.

Tombstone suppression was moved to the whole merged set (DropStore.swift:314) rather than only the cloud branch — this correctly closes the round-3 hole where a locally-present row could resurrect a drop whose delete was unconfirmed, not just a cloud row.

Test isolation is genuinely fixed: injected UserDefaults suites (DropStore.swift:250, tests makeDefaults/tearDown removePersistentDomain) plus testLibraryPersistenceIsScopedToAnInjectedDefaultsSuite, which asserts the shipping domain stays clean. The actor test doubles (GatedCloudStore/FlakyLocalStore) reproduce production isolation and suspension points instead of the old @MainActor non-suspending stub.

disarmSemanticMatte is installed at all four transition sites that gate frameUpdate off (stop 360, suspend 393, sessionWasInterrupted 2300, didFailWithError 2326), and re-arm is correct without an explicit re-armer: frameUpdate recomputes farMode unconditionally each tick (GeoARSessionManager.swift:2115-2128) and the pass re-attaches via passNeeded (1050-1054), so the SEM chip and the Metal pass both recover once isInterrupted falls in sessionInterruptionEnded (2308).

ShareDropSheet's keep-open-on-terminal onDismiss cannot trap the user: the close button (ShareDropSheet.swift:28) calls the environment dismiss directly and is not routed through the onDismiss guard, and re-tapping the CTA hits the sendLink guard rather than re-presenting the activity sheet. No unreachable branch — the terminal caption is reachable for any drop that failed on a prior attempt.

RootView's global persist banner layers correctly (overlay on the ZStack that already contains NightTabBar, so it draws above it; 96pt bottom padding clears the bar and its -18pt orb offset) and its dismiss-only lifecycle re-triggers properly, because clearPersistError() nils the slot so an identical next error string re-satisfies the `if let` (RootView.swift:126-132, DropStore.swift:408-410).

FirebaseDropStore's notFound-to-success mapping (FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97) is the right shape for a delete seam, and remove(contentsOf:) (DropStore.swift:393-405) correctly accumulates per-item outcomes so one success cannot erase another's failure.

findings.claim: A refused cloud delete now keeps its tombstone forever with no state that can ever retire it: retries stop at 3, nothing clears pendingDeleteIDs except a successful delete, and the set is durable in UserDefaults. This both freezes ProfileScreen on "Finishing N deletions…" permanently and makes the suppression at DropStore.swift:314 a permanent id-level blacklist that silently deletes any drop that legitimately reappears under that id.
findings.evidence: reconcileCloud stops retrying at `(deleteAttempts[id] ?? 0) < 3` (DropStore.swift:423-426); the catch in launchCloudDelete only increments the counter and deliberately keeps the tombstone (491-499); clearPendingDelete is called only on success (487); markPendingDelete persists to the durable pendingDeleteDropIDs key (526-529, 536-538). refresh() then applies `for id in pendingDeleteIDs { merged[id] = nil }` to the WHOLE merged set (314). ProfileScreen.swift:99-105 renders "Finishing N deletions…" for any non-empty pendingDeleteIDs and sits above the Synced branch (106-113), so it permanently hides "Synced". The trigger is the common case, not an edge case: launchCloudDelete builds a bare ghost with no ownerUid (483-484) and fires delete at a document that was never uploaded (drop created offline / pre-auth), and per the stated platform fact an owner-gated rules delete of a nonexistent doc is permission-denied, not notFound — so the FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97 notFound mapping never fires and every such delete is a permanent refusal. Round 3 cleared the tombstone here; round 4 both made it permanent and added the UI branch that renders it.
findings.failureScenario: User creates a drop in airplane mode (or before anon auth resolves), then deletes it from the Sent tab. Local delete succeeds; launchCloudDelete fires at drops/<id> which does not exist; rules evaluate resource == null and return permission-denied. The tombstone is kept and persisted. Three refused attempts later retries stop. From that moment on, on this launch and every future launch, the Profile chip reads "Finishing 1 deletion…" and the user never sees "Synced" again, with no action available to resolve it. Second consequence: the user later re-opens their own share link for that same drop; ReceiveScreen reinstates it via RootView.swift:63 and it renders in AR — then the next refresh() runs `merged[id] = nil` and the drop vanishes from the library permanently, with no error shown, because a months-old stale tombstone is still in UserDefaults.
findings.proposedFix: Give a delete a terminal state the same way a write got one. When deleteAttempts[id] reaches the budget, move the id out of pendingDeleteIDs into a separate durable `suppressedDeleteIDs` set that still feeds the merge suppression at line 314 but is NOT rendered as in-flight, and publish `deletesInFlight` (pendingDeleteIDs minus exhausted ids) for ProfileScreen.swift:99 to key on. Additionally, treat permission-denied on a delete whose document was never acknowledged as satisfied (an id that was still in pendingSyncIDs when remove() ran can never have a server doc), and clear any suppression for an id that is re-added through add()/update() so a re-received drop is not silently deleted.

testCase.name: testExhaustedCloudDeleteStopsCountingAsInFlightAndDoesNotSuppressAReAddedDrop
testCase.steps: Arrange: GatedCloudStore with setFailDelete(permission-denied NSError, for: drop.id) and setLoadResult([]); library = makeLibrary(cloud:defaults:) with an injected suite. add(drop). Act: try await library.remove(drop); drive reconcileCloud() in a loop until `await cloud.deleteAttempts >= 3` and no further attempts occur after two more reconcile passes; then await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert (1) library.deletesInFlight.isEmpty — the exhausted tombstone must not read as in-progress (this is what ProfileScreen.swift:99 keys on); (2) suppression still holds: with cloud.setLoadResult([drop]) a refresh does not resurrect it. Act 2: a re-add of the same id — var received = drop; received.receivedViaLink = true; try await library.update(received, persist: true); await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert (3) library.drops.contains { $0.id == drop.id } — a drop deliberately re-added must not be erased by a stale tombstone.
testCase.infrastructure: Existing GatedCloudStore (setFailDelete, deleteAttempts) and makeDefaults()/makeLibrary(cloud:defaults:) suffice. Requires DropLibrary to expose a published `deletesInFlight` (or equivalent non-terminal delete count) and to clear suppression on re-add — both part of the fix.

findings.claim: Moving startWrap from didReact to reactionDelivered makes the entire wrap→Memory payoff depend on a Firestore server ack, which per the stated platform fact is never delivered while offline — so a reaction sent with no connectivity leaves the pill stuck on "Sending…" forever, the wrap countdown never appears, and MemoryScreen (the loop's payoff) becomes unreachable.
findings.evidence: startWrap(seconds: 15) now runs only inside reactionDelivered() (ReactionSession.swift:53-57); didReact only latches sentEmoji and delivery = .sending (47-50). The only caller of reactionDelivered/reactionFailed is the Task at ReactionSession.swift:165-172, which awaits ReactionService.send → FirestoreAcked.setData (ReactionService.swift:46-51) → withCheckedThrowingContinuation on setData's completion (FirestoreAcked.swift:19-33). Firestore does not invoke write completions while offline, so neither branch of the do/catch ever runs: delivery stays .sending, phase stays .watching, and RootView's memory cover — gated on `reactionSession.phase == .memory` (RootView.swift:75-78) — never presents, so memorySnapshot is never captured either. Round 3 started the wrap synchronously in didReact, so this is a regression introduced by this round, in the field condition an outdoor AR app spends most of its time in.
findings.failureScenario: Receiver walks to a drop in a low-signal spot, opens the magic link, watches the drop, taps ❤️. The pill reads "Sending to Sam…" and never changes. No "SESSION WRAPS IN 15 S" chip ever appears, so "hold to keep watching" is meaningless, no Memory screen with the snapshot and the "send one back" CTA is ever shown. The only exit is the X (ReactionOverlay line 121-130), which calls endSession() → .idle, skipping the Memory phase entirely. The product's payoff moment is silently deleted, and the user is left with a permanent "Sending…" claim.
findings.proposedFix: Decouple ritual timing from delivery truth: start the wrap in didReact() (as round 3 did) and let `delivery` alone carry honesty — the pill can read "Sending…"/"Sent"/"Couldn't send" while the countdown runs independently. If the wrap must not start before an outcome, bound the wait: race the ack against a timeout in the ReactionOverlay Task (e.g. 8s) and call a new session.reactionQueued() on expiry, which starts the wrap and shows "Will send when you're back online". Either way, phase must never be able to remain .watching indefinitely because of a network condition.

testCase.name: testWrapAndMemoryStillReachWhenTheReactionAckNeverArrives
testCase.steps: Arrange: @MainActor ReactionSession; session.startWatching(GeoDrop()); a GatedReactionSender double whose send(_:to:from:) parks on a continuation the test never resumes (mirroring an offline Firestore completion). Act: bind the overlay's send path to the double, call session.didReact("❤️"), then advance the wrap clock (inject a Clock/sleep seam, or assert on the deadline rather than sleeping 15s). Assert: within one second session.phase is .wrapping (the countdown started without an ack); session.delivery == .sending and deliveryText reads "Sending to …", never "Sent to …"; after the wrap window elapses session.phase == .memory so RootView's memory cover can present. Assert the parked send is still unresolved throughout — the payoff must not depend on it.
testCase.infrastructure: New: a `ReactionSending` protocol extracted from ReactionService (send throws) so ReactionOverlay/tests can inject; a GatedReactionSender actor double with a park/release continuation gate, modelled on the round-4 GatedCloudStore. Also a test seam for the 15s wrap duration (inject seconds or a Clock) so the case does not sleep in real time.

findings.claim: The reaction delivery state is a single shared last-writer-wins slot with no per-send generation — the exact defect class round 4 eliminated in DropLibrary via syncGenerations. Each emoji tap spawns an independent unordered Task, so a stale send's outcome overwrites the newer send's state and the pill lies in both directions.
findings.evidence: Every tap runs `withAnimation { session.didReact(emoji) }` then a fresh detached `Task { try await reactions.send(...); session.reactionDelivered() } catch { session.reactionFailed() }` (ReactionSession.swift:162-172). didReact unconditionally overwrites sentEmoji and sets delivery = .sending (47-50); reactionDelivered/reactionFailed unconditionally overwrite delivery (53-62). Nothing correlates an outcome with the emoji that produced it — no token, no sequence number, no cancellation of the previous send. Contrast DropStore.swift:443 and 455/461/470/475, where the same round explicitly refuses to let a superseded write report an outcome. reactionDelivered also calls startWrap only when phase is still .watching (55), so ordering additionally determines whether the wrap ever starts.
findings.failureScenario: Viewer taps ❤️; the write is slow (it will eventually be rejected by rules). Half a second later they tap 😂; that write succeeds quickly. reactionDelivered() fires: pill reads "😂 Sent to Sam", wrap starts. Then the ❤️ task finally fails: reactionFailed() fires, delivery flips to .failed, and the pill now reads "😂 Couldn't send — tap an emoji to retry" in coral while the wrap countdown continues — telling the user the reaction that actually landed did not, and inviting a duplicate send. Reversed ordering is worse: a failed 😂 followed by a late-arriving ❤️ success renders "😂 Sent to Sam" for a reaction the server rejected, which is the precise lie this round set out to remove.
findings.proposedFix: Give each send a token: `private var deliveryToken = 0`; didReact increments it and returns the token; reactionDelivered(token:)/reactionFailed(token:) guard `token == deliveryToken` before touching delivery or starting the wrap. Pass the token through the overlay Task at ReactionSession.swift:165. Optionally also cancel the previous in-flight send task on a new tap, so a superseded write is not issued at all (mirroring enqueueCloudSync's syncTasks[id]?.cancel() at DropStore.swift:445).

testCase.name: testStaleReactionOutcomeCannotOverwriteTheNewerTapsDeliveryState
testCase.steps: Arrange: @MainActor ReactionSession after startWatching(drop); GatedReactionSender that parks each send and can resume a specific one with a specific outcome. Act: tap ❤️ (didReact + send A parked), then tap 😂 (didReact + send B parked); resume B with success → session.reactionDelivered(token: tokenB); then resume A with a rejection → session.reactionFailed(token: tokenA). Assert: session.sentEmoji == "😂"; session.delivery == .delivered (the stale failure was ignored); the pill text resolves to "Sent to <sender>". Reverse case in the same test: fresh session, tap ❤️ then 😂, resolve B as failure and A as success — assert session.delivery == .failed, i.e. a stale success never claims delivery for a rejected emoji. Also assert startWrap fired exactly once.
testCase.infrastructure: Same GatedReactionSender/ReactionSending seam as the previous case, extended with releaseOne(success:) so two parked sends can be resolved in a chosen order. Requires the token-carrying reactionDelivered(token:)/reactionFailed(token:) signatures from the fix; the test asserts on ReactionSession state directly, no SwiftUI host needed.

findings.claim: The orphan reap's "provably clean load" predicate is `localReadWarning == nil`, which a MISSING store file satisfies. LocalDropStore reports an absent file as a perfectly clean, empty load, so a launch where the store file is gone but the persisted outbox is not reaps and permanently destroys the entire outbox — the round-2 C1 bug reintroduced behind a guard that does not actually prove a successful read.
findings.evidence: loadDrops' first branch sets `pendingReadWarning = nil` and returns [] for a non-existent file (DropStore.swift:85-91); it writes no incident note (the comment at 86-88 claims the journal covers this, but the journal only exists if THIS file path was previously quarantined — a vanished container takes drops.json.incident with it). lastLoadReadWarning() then returns nil (158-164), refresh() assigns localReadWarning = nil (288-292), and the reap at 321-327 clears every pending id whose row is absent, calling clearPending → persistSet, which rewrites the durable pendingSyncDropIDs key to the empty list (509-512, 536-538). Round 4's own test pins the buggy behaviour: testPendingIDForAnUnloadableDropDoesNotStayUploadingForever seeds a pending ghost id, builds a library over a temporary URL that was never written, refreshes, and asserts the id was reaped — i.e. it asserts that a load of a file that does not exist is proof the drop is gone.
findings.failureScenario: User creates three drops with no connectivity; all three land on disk and all three ids are persisted to pendingSyncDropIDs awaiting the auth-ready re-push. The Application Support container is subsequently relocated or the store file otherwise fails to be present at next launch (restore-to-new-device, container migration, a failed atomic rename leaving the file missing). On relaunch, refresh() reads an absent file, reports it clean, sees an empty drops array, and reaps all three ids — silently discarding the entire outbox with a log line and no user-visible state. The drops are never uploaded and any share link handed out for them is dead forever, which is exactly the class of failure the pending pipeline exists to prevent.
findings.proposedFix: Make LocalDropStore distinguish 'read a real file cleanly' from 'there was nothing to read'. Add a stored `lastLoadWasReadOfExistingStore: Bool` (false for the absent-file branch, the quarantine branch and the throwing-read branch; true only after a successful decode with zero skipped rows) and expose it alongside lastLoadReadWarning(). Gate the reap at DropStore.swift:321 on that flag rather than on `localReadWarning == nil`. Update testPendingIDForAnUnloadableDropDoesNotStayUploadingForever so its arrange step writes a real empty `[]` store file before asserting the reap.

testCase.name: testMissingStoreFileIsNotProofADropIsGoneAndDoesNotReapTheOutbox
testCase.steps: Arrange: injected defaults suite with defaults.set([ghostA.uuidString, ghostB.uuidString], forKey: "pendingSyncDropIDs"); a LocalDropStore over a temporaryFile() URL that is deliberately NOT created; library = makeLibrary(local: thatStore, defaults: suite). Act: await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert: library.pendingSyncIDs still contains both ghosts, and defaults.stringArray(forKey: "pendingSyncDropIDs") still contains both — a store that was never read must never retire the outbox. Second half: write `[]` to that URL (a genuine, clean, empty store), refresh again, and NOW assert both ghosts are reaped and the defaults key is empty — the reap must still work on a real clean read.
testCase.infrastructure: Existing makeDefaults()/makeLibrary(local:defaults:) helpers and temporaryFile(). Requires the new LocalDropStore read-provenance accessor from the fix (exposed as an actor method so DropLibrary can await it, alongside lastLoadReadWarning).

findings.claim: The refresh() local-read-failure path writes published state after an unguarded await, violating the very invariant this round claims ("re-checks it after EVERY await and aborts if it was superseded"). A superseded, failed refresh can overwrite a newer successful refresh's clean localReadWarning with a stale unreadable-store warning — which additionally disables the orphan reap that keys on it.
findings.evidence: In the catch branch the generation is checked (DropStore.swift:279) and then `localReadWarning = await localStore.lastLoadReadWarning()` assigns to published state directly across a suspension point with no re-check (280-282), followed by the fallback assignment at 283-285. The success path immediately below gets this right — `let warning = await localStore.lastLoadReadWarning(); guard refreshGeneration == generation else { return }; localReadWarning = warning` (288-292) — so the two paths disagree about the discipline. The consequence compounds because the reap at 321 is gated on `localReadWarning == nil`. Note also that both sites reach the warning through a concrete downcast `local as? LocalDropStore` (280, 288), so the round-4 test double FlakyLocalStore can never exercise this code — testFailingLocalReadNeitherHidesTheFailureNorClearsState falls through to the hardcoded fallback string at 284 and therefore does not cover the defect at all.
findings.failureScenario: Refresh A begins while the store is momentarily unreadable (data-protection window, transient I/O error) and enters the catch branch, then suspends inside lastLoadReadWarning(). Before it resumes, the auth-ready task fires (RootView.swift:155-158) and refresh B runs: the transient is gone, B reads local successfully, sets localReadWarning = nil, publishes fresh drops and reaps correctly. A then resumes and writes "Your saved drops couldn't be read — pull to retry" over B's clean state. The Sent tab's questionmark.folder banner (DropsListScreen.swift:58-60) now claims the library is unreadable while the library is fine, the banner cannot be dismissed, and every subsequent refresh that starts before it is overwritten skips the orphan reap because localReadWarning is non-nil.
findings.proposedFix: Mirror the success path exactly: `let warning = await (local as? LocalDropStore)?.lastLoadReadWarning(); guard refreshGeneration == generation else { return }; localReadWarning = warning ?? "Your saved drops couldn't be read — pull to retry"`. Separately, replace the `as? LocalDropStore` downcasts at 280 and 288 with a protocol requirement (e.g. `ReadWarningReporting` refining DropStore, with a default nil implementation) so a test double can drive this path at all.

testCase.name: testSupersededFailingRefreshCannotOverwriteANewerRefreshsCleanReadWarning
testCase.steps: Arrange: GatedLocalStore (actor conforming to DropStore + ReadWarningReporting) with setThrowOnLoad(true), a warning string of "stale unreadable", and a gate that parks lastLoadReadWarning() calls; library = makeLibrary(local: gated). Act: launch refresh A in a Task; waitUntil the store reports one parked warning call; now set the store healthy (setThrowOnLoad(false), warning nil, rows [drop]) and `await library.refresh(near: nil)` to completion as refresh B; then releaseAllWarningReads() and await refresh A. Assert: library.localReadWarning == nil (the stale verdict from the superseded pass never lands), library.drops contains drop, and — with a ghost id seeded in the injected defaults and no matching row — that the reap B performed was not undone.
testCase.infrastructure: New GatedLocalStore actor double with a continuation gate on the warning accessor, modelled on GatedCloudStore's parkedLoads/releaseAllLoads. Requires the ReadWarningReporting protocol from the fix, since the current concrete `as? LocalDropStore` downcast makes this path untestable with any double.

findings.claim: The render-time failed-asset announcement fires inside makeHolder, which runs once per holder CREATION, not once per failure — so it re-fires on every re-placement, and because showPersistError is a single slot that cancels its predecessor's clear task, multiple failed drops in one tick collapse to only the last drop's title. It also duplicates the onAssetLoaded announcement with different wording, and misfires from the room-test path.
findings.evidence: makeHolder announces unconditionally whenever DropEntityFactory.isAssetFailed is true (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1517-1520). makeHolder is called from three places, each only when placedHolders[id] == nil: the pedestrian tick (1454), the transit tick (1959) and the room test (511). Holders are pruned whenever a drop leaves the tick's drop set (1478-1489, 1965-1976), and that set is a radius filter over library.drops — so ordinary GPS jitter or walking around the boundary destroys and re-creates the holder, re-entering makeHolder and re-firing the toast every time. showPersistError overwrites persistErrorText and cancels the pending 4s clear task (84-95), so N failed drops placed in the same tick produce N calls and only the last title survives; and the parallel subscriber at 321-325 announces the same failure as the generic "A 3D model couldn't be loaded", so one broken USDZ can produce two differently-worded toasts. The room-test path (505-511) names a synthetic drop the user never created.
findings.failureScenario: A user with two drops whose USDZ files failed to decode at launch walks a route where both sit near the render radius. Each time the pair re-enters range, two showPersistError calls land in the same tick; the AR HUD shows only "The 3D model for 'Balloons' couldn't be loaded" and never mentions the second drop. Over a two-minute walk with boundary jitter the same toast reappears eight or ten times, each occurrence resetting the 4s window, so it effectively camps in the status card and blocks the statusText line the user needs for tracking guidance (ARScreen.swift:402-412) — the announcement becomes noise and the user learns to ignore the one channel that also carries "Couldn't save this drop" from RootView.swift:65.
findings.proposedFix: Announce per failed ASSET, once per session, not per placement. Add `private var announcedFailedAssets: Set<String>` to the manager and guard the block at 1517: `guard announcedFailedAssets.insert(assetName).inserted else { }`. Aggregate when several land together ("2 drops' 3D models couldn't be loaded") rather than letting the last writer win, unify the wording with the onAssetLoaded subscriber at 324 so one failure yields one message, and skip the announcement entirely when roomDrops[drop.id] != nil so the room-test path does not name a synthetic drop.

testCase.name: testFailedAssetIsAnnouncedOncePerAssetNotOncePerPlacement
testCase.steps: Arrange: @MainActor GeoARSessionManager; DropEntityFactory._setFailedForTesting(["balloons"]); two GeoDrops with content == .animated and assetName == "balloons". Act: call the extracted announceFailedAssetIfNeeded(for:) for drop A, then drop B, then drop A again (simulating a prune/re-place cycle). Assert: manager.persistErrorText is non-nil after the first call; a recorded announcement count (or a test-visible announcedFailedAssets set) equals 1, not 3; the message aggregates both drops rather than naming only the last. Second act: with roomDrops[roomDrop.id] set, call the same entry point for a room-test drop and assert no announcement is emitted.
testCase.infrastructure: New: a @MainActor test-only seam on DropEntityFactory to seed failedAssets (`_setFailedForTesting`) since failedAssets is private and only reachable through a real USDZ decode; extraction of the announcement out of makeHolder into an internal `announceFailedAssetIfNeeded(for:)` so it can be called without an ARView; and a spy on showPersistError (or an exposed announcement counter) to count invocations. No ARSession or device camera required.

additionalTests.name: testTerminalUploadFailureHasAUserReachableRetryFromTheShareSheet
additionalTests.pins: The interaction between ShareDropSheet.swift:184-188 (sendLink refuses to call library.update for any drop in terminalSyncFailureIDs) and DropStore.swift:440-442 (enqueueCloudSync deliberately clears terminal to 'give a previously terminal drop one more chance'). Because terminalSyncFailureIDs is durable across launches (DropStore.swift:259-260, 514-517), the share sheet's guard permanently removes the only retry affordance on the surface where the user is actually trying to act — the 'one more chance' path is unreachable from there. Round 4 shipped both halves and pinned neither; this test fixes the intended contract before the guard and the clearTerminal comment drift further apart.
additionalTests.steps: Arrange: GatedCloudStore with setFailSave(DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount, for: drop.id); library = makeLibrary(cloud:defaults:); try await library.add(drop); waitUntil library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id). Act 1: call the retry entry point the share sheet should offer — library.retryTerminalSync(drop) — and assert terminalSyncFailureIDs no longer contains the id and pendingSyncIDs does (a fresh intent re-arms the write). additionalTests.name: testSemanticMatteDisarmsOnInterruptionAndReArmsWhenTheInterruptionEnds
additionalTests.pins: The full disarm/re-arm cycle for the round-4 arui-4 change: disarmSemanticMatte (GeoARSessionManager.swift:376-380) at all four transition sites (360, 393, 2300, 2326) and the implicit re-arm that nobody writes explicitly — frameUpdate recomputing farMode each tick (2115-2128) plus the pass reattaching via passNeeded (1050-1054) once isInterrupted falls at 2308. Today nothing asserts that the SEM chip (ARScreen.swift:384-386) recovers after an interruption ends, so a future gating change to frameUpdate would silently leave semantic occlusion off for the rest of the session with no test failing.

Act 1: call sessionWasInterrupted(session) and await the main-actor hop. Assert: semanticMatteArmed == false, semanticFeed.setEnabled(false) was recorded, pass.setCallbacksActive(false) was recorded, and further frameUpdate ticks change none of it (the isInterrupted guard at 2038 holds). Act 2: call sessionInterruptionEnded(session), await the hop, then tick frameUpdate with the same far holder still placed. Assert: semanticMatteArmed == true again, semanticFeed.setEnabled(true) recorded, pass.setCallbacksActive(true) recorded — the SEM chip recovers without any explicit re-armer. Repeat Act 1/Act 2 for the suspend()/resumeSession() pair to cover the second disarm site.

soundAreas: Write-pipeline generation discipline is now genuinely closed: the entry check at DropStore.swift:455 stops a superseded task from even issuing its write, and every post-await mutation re-checks (461/470/475). The gated actor double pins it deterministically (DropStoreTests testSupersededSyncTaskCannotClearPendingWhenItFinallyResumes) — a stale generation's late ack can no longer clear its successor's pending flag.

Publish-path generation guards are correct on the paths that matter (DropStore.swift:273, 290, 296, 305, 307): a mutation during an in-flight refresh supersedes the whole pass, and testDeleteDuringRefreshIsNotResurrectedByThePublish drives the interleaving with a real parked continuation rather than a sleep.

The refresh abort-on-unreadable-local-truth (DropStore.swift:271-287) is the right call and is honestly reported: in-memory drops and pendingSyncIDs survive an aborted pass, and LocalDropStore.save() still rethrows a failed read (DropStore.swift:169) so the library can never be atomically erased by one bad read.

The incident journal solves the real problem for the quarantine case: the verdict is written at the moment of destruction (DropStore.swift:131) and the transient slot is cleared (130), so the next load — which sees no file because the quarantine moved it — cannot read as clean (158-164). Clearing only on a clean AND non-empty library (112-118) is the right predicate, and the two-load sequence is pinned by testWholeFileQuarantineWarningSurvivesSubsequentLoads.

Test-harness upgrade is real and load-bearing: injected UserDefaults suites with per-test domains removed (DropStoreTests makeDefaults/tearDown) mean the suite can no longer corrupt the shipping outbox, and the actor doubles (GatedCloudStore/FlakyLocalStore) reproduce production isolation and suspension points instead of testing a non-existent synchronous program.

The single acked-write seam is a genuine consolidation: FirestoreAcked.swift:15-35 is the only continuation, the duplicate copies in FirebaseDropStore and AccountService are gone, and the reaction path — the one that was silently staging locally — now routes through it (ReactionService.swift:695-701 of the diff).

Batch delete aggregation (DropStore.swift:393-405) with DropsListScreen.swift:107 wiring is correct: per-item outcomes accumulate and the aggregate is written last, so a later success cannot erase an earlier failure, and testFailedDeleteInABatchStaysReported pins both the banner text and the surviving row.

The arui-4 semantic-matte claim holds. All four transition sites disarm (GeoARSessionManager.swift:360, 393, 2300, 2326), and the disarm is not sticky: frameUpdate recomputes farMode unconditionally (2115-2128) and the governor re-attaches the pass callbacks (1050-1054) on resume, so occlusion is not silently dead for the rest of the session.

The arui-1 render-time asset check genuinely closes the preload-before-attach gap: DropEntityFactory.isAssetFailed queried inside makeHolder (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1517-1520) survives a decode that completed before the session manager or its callback existed.

ShareDropSheet's ranking is correctly ordered — the terminal caption outranks both the pending and the generic reassurance (ShareDropSheet.swift:135-155) and sendLink refuses to present the activity sheet at all (184-188) — and FirebaseDropStore.delete's notFound-to-success mapping (FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97) is the right shape for the cases it can actually observe.

findings.claim: A refused cloud delete keeps its tombstone forever — nothing ever retires it — so pendingDeleteIDs becomes permanent durable state, "Synced" becomes unreachable, the Profile chip claims a deletion is in progress for the life of the install, and each launch burns three more denied writes.
findings.evidence: The catch arm at DropStore.swift:491-499 increments deleteAttempts and logs, but never calls clearPendingDelete and never records exhaustion. deleteAttempts is an in-memory dictionary (DropStore.swift:235), so the `< 3` bound at DropStore.swift:423-424 resets on every launch while pendingDeleteIDs is persisted (DropStore.swift:526-533). ProfileScreen.swift:99-105 renders pendingDeleteIDs as "Finishing N deletion(s)…", and it sits directly above the "Synced" branch at 106-113, so "Synced" is unreachable while any tombstone survives. The notFound-to-success mapping at FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97 does not cover the dominant case: per the platform facts, deleting a doc that was never uploaded under owner-gated rules returns permission-denied (resource == null), not notFound — so the exact case round 4 says it handles falls into the keep-forever arm. Round 3 cleared the tombstone here; round 4 removed the clear without adding a retirement path.
findings.failureScenario: User creates a drop in airplane mode (never uploaded; local row only), then swipes it away in Sent. remove() persists the tombstone and fires launchCloudDelete. Back online, Firestore refuses with permission-denied (no such doc under owner-gated rules), so the tombstone stays. Three retries per session are spent, then stop; on every subsequent launch reconcileCloud spends three more denied writes forever. Profile permanently reads "Finishing 1 deletion…" and can never read "Synced" again, on a device whose library is fully uploaded. Repeat over months of offline creates and the persisted pendingDeleteDropIDs array grows without bound. Second consequence: round 4 moved suppression from the cloud loop to the whole merged set (DropStore.swift:314), so if that same drop id ever legitimately reappears locally — the sharer re-sends the link, ReceiveScreen saves it to disk via library.update — the next refresh deletes it from the published set and it is invisible in every screen while sitting on disk.
findings.proposedFix: Retire the tombstone when retries are exhausted instead of keeping it forever: persist deleteAttempts alongside the id, and on exhaustion move the id out of pendingDeleteIDs into a separate durable `abandonedDeleteIDs` set that still suppresses resurrection but is not rendered as work-in-progress. Better, distinguish the never-uploaded case at the store seam — if the drop was still in pendingSyncIDs when remove() ran, the server never had it, so map permission-denied on delete to success exactly as notFound is mapped (FirebaseDropStore.swift:90). Also scope suppression to the cloud loop again, or clear the tombstone when a local row for that id is re-saved, so a legitimately re-added drop is not silently hidden.

testCase.name: testRefusedCloudDeleteStopsClaimingDeletionInProgressAndStopsRetrying
testCase.steps: Arrange: injected UserDefaults suite; GatedCloudStore with setFailDelete(NSError(FirestoreErrorDomain, code: permissionDenied), for: drop.id) and setLoadResult([drop]); add(drop). Act: try await library.remove(drop), then call library.reconcileCloud() five times with waits between, so the per-session bound is exhausted. Assert: (1) cloud.deleteAttempts stops at the bound (never grows past it); (2) library.pendingDeleteIDs no longer contains the id once retries are exhausted, so the Profile chip's source is empty and the "Synced" branch is reachable; (3) the drop still does not resurrect after await library.refresh(near: nil) — suppression survives via the abandoned set; (4) construct a SECOND DropLibrary over the SAME injected defaults (relaunch) and assert it does not resume unbounded retries: cloud.deleteAttempts is unchanged after its refresh; (5) after the id is retired, saving a fresh local row with that same id and refreshing publishes it (no silent suppression).
testCase.infrastructure: Existing GatedCloudStore (add a delete-attempt counter per id, already present) plus the injected-defaults helper; needs the second-library-over-same-defaults relaunch pattern, which no current test uses.

findings.claim: enqueueCloudSync clears the durable terminal marker at enqueue time, before the retry has been attempted — so any edit of a terminal drop that does not reach the server (offline is the normal case) permanently destroys the terminal truth and downgrades the drop to a reassuring "Uploading…", re-arming exactly the dead-link share that flows-3 was built to stop.
findings.evidence: DropStore.swift:439-442 marks pending and calls clearTerminal(drop.id) before the write is issued; clearTerminal (519-524) also erases syncFailureReasons and rewrites the persisted terminalSyncDropIDs array, so the loss survives relaunch. The success path already clears terminal after the ack (DropStore.swift:463), making the enqueue-time clear redundant for the good case and destructive for the bad one. Per the platform facts, Firestore write completions are not invoked while offline, so cloud.save suspends indefinitely and neither the ownedByAnotherAccount arm (467) nor any other arm ever runs. The trigger is a routine gesture: an AR height-slider commit calls library.update (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1636). With terminal cleared, ShareDropSheet.swift:184 stops blocking sendLink and 144-150 shows "Still uploading — the link starts working once your drop reaches the cloud".
findings.failureScenario: Anonymous account is replaced (new uid); five old drops go terminal and Profile honestly says "5 drops can't sync from this account connection". In the field, offline, the user nudges one drop's height in AR. update() → enqueueCloudSync → clearTerminal: the id is removed from terminalSyncFailureIDs AND from the persisted terminalSyncDropIDs, and added to pendingSyncIDs. Profile now says "Uploading 1 drop…" for a drop that can never upload; the Sent banner drops to 4. The user opens Share on it: the coral terminal warning is gone, the gold "still uploading, the link starts working soon" caption is shown, sendLink's guard passes, and a permanently dead magic link is handed to a friend. Kill the app and relaunch: the terminal state is gone from disk, so the drop presents as merely pending forever.
findings.proposedFix: Delete the clearTerminal call at DropStore.swift:442. A retry does not disprove the mismatch — only a server ack does, and that is already handled at line 463. If the UI needs to show that a retry is in flight, add a separate transient `retryingIDs` set that renders below the terminal ranking rather than replacing it, so terminal keeps outranking "Synced"/"Uploading" in Profile, Sent, and ShareDropSheet until the server actually accepts the write.

testCase.name: testEditingATerminalDropKeepsItTerminalUntilTheServerActuallyAccepts
testCase.steps: Arrange: injected defaults; GatedCloudStore.setFailSave(DropStoreError.ownedByAnotherAccount, for: drop.id); try await library.add(drop); waitUntil { library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id) }. Act: await cloud.setGateSaves(true) (models offline: the write parks and never completes), then try await library.update(drop) and waitUntil { await cloud.parkedSaveCount == 1 }. Assert while the write is parked: (1) library.terminalSyncFailureIDs still contains drop.id; (2) defaults.stringArray(forKey: "terminalSyncDropIDs") still contains it; (3) a freshly constructed DropLibrary over the same defaults restores it as terminal (relaunch honesty); (4) library.syncFailureReasons[drop.id] is still non-nil so the ShareDropSheet caption has its text. Then releaseAllSaves() and assert the drop is terminal and not pending after the rejection lands.
testCase.infrastructure: Existing GatedCloudStore save gate plus per-id failure injection and the injected-defaults helper — all present; only the assertions and the second-library relaunch check are new.

findings.claim: Round 4 moved the session wrap from the reaction tap to the server ack, so an offline reaction never wraps: the pill is stuck on "Sending to X…" forever, the Memory screen — the product loop's entire payoff — is unreachable, and the failure state never appears because the awaited write never returns.
findings.evidence: startWrap is now reachable only from reactionDelivered (ReactionSession.swift:53-57); didReact (47-50) only latches sentEmoji and delivery = .sending. The overlay's send task (ReactionSession.swift:165-172) awaits reactions.send, which routes to FirestoreAcked.setData — and per the platform facts a Firestore write completion is not invoked while offline, so neither reactionDelivered nor reactionFailed ever runs. phase therefore stays .watching, and RootView.swift:75-78 presents MemoryScreen only on phase == .memory. There is no timeout anywhere in the class. deliveryText (ReactionSession.swift:202-208) renders "Sending to X…" indefinitely, so the "tap an emoji to retry" affordance at 206 is never shown. Round 3's didReact started the 15 s wrap unconditionally; this is a regression introduced by the honesty fix.
findings.failureScenario: Recipient opens a magic link in a basement/subway/airplane-mode spot — the exact place a geo-drop is opened — reveals the drop in AR, and taps a heart. Firebase auth is warm (anonymous uid survives in the keychain, so send does not fast-fail on notSignedIn) and the write stages locally with no completion. The pill reads "Sending to sender…" for as long as the user stands there. No countdown chip appears, phase never leaves .watching, so the wrap → Memory transition never happens and the user never gets the memory card, the "send one back" CTA, or any indication of failure. The only exit is the X button (ReactionSession.swift:122), which calls endSession and discards the memory entirely. The sender's loop payoff is silently deleted by the same change that was supposed to make delivery honest.
findings.proposedFix: Restore the wrap on didReact — optimistic progression is not a delivery claim, and the pill already carries the honest wording. Keep "Sent" gated on the ack, and add a bounded delivery timeout (e.g. 8-10 s) that flips delivery to .failed (or a .queued state with "will send when you're back online") so the retry copy is reachable. The wrap countdown and the Memory screen must never depend on network I/O.

testCase.name: testOfflineReactionStillWrapsToMemoryAndNeverClaimsDelivery
testCase.steps: Arrange: ReactionSession with an injected wrap duration (e.g. 1 s) and an injected Reacting seam whose send(_:to:from:) never returns; session.startWatching(dropA). Act: session.didReact("❤️") and drive the overlay's send path against the never-returning double; advance past the wrap duration with waitUntil. Assert: (1) session.delivery == .sending immediately after the tap and never becomes .delivered; (2) session.phase transitions .watching → .wrapping → .memory despite no ack, i.e. the payoff is not gated on the network; (3) after the delivery timeout elapses, session.delivery == .failed so the "tap an emoji to retry" copy is reachable; (4) a subsequent tap re-enters .sending without restarting the wrap twice.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs two small seams that do not exist yet: injectable wrap/timeout durations on ReactionSession (constants today, 15 s hard-coded at line 56) and a `Reacting` protocol so ReactionService can be replaced with a never-returning double. ReactionSession is already @MainActor and otherwise unit-testable.

findings.claim: The reaction send task is unstructured and its completion is applied to whatever drop the shared session is watching when it finally returns — so a late ack for a previous drop starts a wrap, and drives the Memory screen, on a drop the user never reacted to.
findings.evidence: ReactionSession.swift:165-172 captures the drop only for the send argument; the completion calls session.reactionDelivered()/reactionFailed() with no identity check, and session is the app-wide @EnvironmentObject ReactionSession (RootView.swift:13/24). startWatching (ReactionSession.swift:29-36) resets sentEmoji and delivery but holds no handle on the in-flight task and cannot cancel it. reactionDelivered (53-57) then calls startWrap whenever phase is .watching, regardless of which drop that phase belongs to. Round 4 created this exposure by turning a fire-and-forget send into a completion that mutates session state.
findings.failureScenario: User opens link A offline, taps a heart (send parks in the Firestore continuation), gives up and closes the overlay, then opens link B from another friend and starts watching. Connectivity returns; A's write finally acks and the orphaned task calls session.reactionDelivered() on B's session: delivery flips to .delivered and a 15 s wrap starts on B. Fifteen seconds later B's session auto-transitions to .memory and RootView presents MemoryScreen for B with myReaction == nil — the user is handed a wrap-up for a drop they were still watching and never reacted to, and the AR moment is terminated under them. The mirror case is equally visible: A's rejection calls reactionFailed() and paints "Couldn't send — tap an emoji to retry" over B's genuinely delivered reaction.
findings.proposedFix: Make the completion identity-addressed: change the callbacks to reactionDelivered(for: UUID) / reactionFailed(for: UUID) and no-op when session.drop?.id != id. Additionally store the send Task on the session and cancel it in startWatching and endSession, so a stale send cannot outlive the session that issued it.

testCase.name: testAckForAPreviousDropNeverTouchesTheCurrentSession
testCase.steps: Arrange: ReactionSession; session.startWatching(dropA); session.didReact("❤️") with the send parked on a gated double. Act: session.startWatching(dropB) (fresh watch), then release dropA's send so its completion fires reactionDelivered(for: dropA.id). Assert: (1) session.delivery is nil (B has no reaction) — not .delivered; (2) session.phase is still .watching for B — no wrap was started; (3) after the wrap interval elapses, session.phase has not become .memory; (4) the symmetric case: releasing dropA's send as a failure leaves session.delivery unchanged for B. Also assert startWatching cancels the outstanding send task so the double observes cancellation.
testCase.infrastructure: Same `Reacting` protocol double with a release gate as the previous case, plus the new id-carrying callback signatures; pure ReactionSession unit test, no UI harness needed once the overlay's completion routes identity through the session.

findings.claim: terminalSyncFailureIDs is durable but has no reaper — the exact orphan problem round 4 fixed for pendingSyncIDs — so a terminal id whose drop no longer exists produces a permanent, undismissable "N drops can't sync" banner counting drops the user cannot find or delete.
findings.evidence: The reap at DropStore.swift:321-327 covers pendingSyncIDs only. terminalSyncFailureIDs is restored from defaults at init (DropStore.swift:259-260) and its only clearers are remove() (383) — which requires the row to exist so the user can swipe it — and a successful cloud save (463), which is by definition impossible for a terminal drop. Both surfaces render a bare count with no per-drop identification: ProfileScreen.swift:82-87 and DropsListScreen.swift:39-47 (the Sent banner is rendered above the ContentUnavailableView, and the padding condition at DropsListScreen.swift:66-70 does not even include terminalSyncFailureIDs, so the sole-banner case renders with zero vertical padding).
findings.failureScenario: Account is replaced; three drops go terminal. drops.json is later corrupted and quarantined (DropStore.swift:120-133), so every local row is gone and the library is empty. terminalSyncDropIDs still holds three ids in UserDefaults. Sent now shows "No drops yet" under an orange "3 drops can't sync from this account connection", Profile shows the same count instead of "Synced", and there is no drop to swipe, no row to tap, and no dismiss control — the banner is permanent for the life of the install. The count is also unattributable in the normal case: with twelve drops in Sent and "2 drops can't sync", no row carries any indicator, so the user cannot tell which two links are dead.
findings.proposedFix: Reap terminal ids under the same provably-clean-load rule already used for pending (DropStore.swift:321): after a clean local load, drop any terminal id with no corresponding row, and skip the reap when localReadWarning is non-nil. Separately, render the state per row in DropsListScreen (a small xmark.icloud badge on DropRow when library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id)) so the aggregate banner is actionable, and add terminalSyncFailureIDs to the banner padding condition at DropsListScreen.swift:68.

testCase.name: testTerminalIDsWithNoSurvivingDropAreRetiredOnlyAfterACleanLoad
testCase.steps: Arrange: injected defaults seeded with terminalSyncDropIDs = [ghostID]; empty, clean LocalDropStore over a temp file. Act: await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert: library.terminalSyncFailureIDs is empty and defaults no longer lists ghostID, so neither banner can outlive its drops. Second half (symmetry with the pending reaper): rebuild the library with the same seed but a local store whose load reports an incident (FlakyLocalStore/journaled warning), refresh, and assert terminalSyncFailureIDs STILL contains ghostID — an unreadable library must never be treated as proof the drop is gone. Third: with a real terminal drop present on disk, refresh and assert the id survives.
testCase.infrastructure: Existing FlakyLocalStore plus injected defaults; needs the local double to also report a read warning through a diagnostics seam (see the abort-path finding) to drive the second half.

findings.claim: The local-read-failure abort path publishes the result of an await straight into @Published state without the generation re-check the round-4 class contract promises for every await, so a superseded failing refresh can stamp a stale error banner over a library that has already healed.
findings.evidence: The class doc at DropStore.swift:196-198 states "an in-flight refresh re-checks it after every await before touching published state", and every other site obeys it: 273, 290 (which correctly binds `let warning = await …` then guards before assigning), 296, 305, 307. Line 281 breaks the pattern — `localReadWarning = await localStore.lastLoadReadWarning()` assigns the awaited value directly, with the generation checked only before the await at 279. The follow-up default at 283-285 compounds it by writing a second time on the same unguarded path.
findings.failureScenario: Refresh A hits a transient read failure (file protection / temporary I/O error) and suspends on lastLoadReadWarning(). During that suspension the user creates a drop, which succeeds (add bumps refreshGeneration) and triggers refresh B; B loads cleanly, clears the incident file, and publishes localReadWarning = nil with the healthy drop list. A then resumes and assigns its stale non-nil warning, so Sent shows "Your saved drops couldn't be read" (or the pull-to-retry fallback) sitting above a correct, fully populated list. Because nothing recomputes the banner until the next refresh, the user is told their library is unreadable while looking at it — the precise class of dishonesty this round exists to eliminate, and it survives whatever period passes before another refresh.
findings.proposedFix: Mirror the correct site at DropStore.swift:288-291: bind the awaited value to a local, `guard refreshGeneration == generation else { return }`, then assign — and apply the same guard before the fallback assignment at 283. While in there, extract lastLoadReadWarning() behind a small protocol (e.g. `DropStoreDiagnostics`) instead of the `as? LocalDropStore` cast at 280/288, so the path is reachable from test doubles at all.

testCase.name: testAbortedRefreshCannotPublishAStaleReadWarningOverAHealedLibrary
testCase.steps: Arrange: local double conforming to the new DropStoreDiagnostics seam, configured to throw on load and to PARK inside lastLoadReadWarning() on a test gate. Act: start refresh A (Task) and wait until the warning read is parked; then heal the double (loads succeed, diagnostics report nil), call try await library.add(drop) (bumps the generation) and await a full refresh B; finally release A's gate and await A. Assert: (1) library.localReadWarning is nil — A's stale warning was discarded; (2) library.drops still contains the added drop (B's publish stands); (3) the mirror ordering — release A before B runs — still ends with B's nil warning winning.
testCase.infrastructure: Needs the diagnostics protocol seam extracted (today the abort path only reads a warning when the store is concretely LocalDropStore, so no double can exercise it) plus a continuation gate on the double's warning accessor, in the same style as GatedCloudStore.

additionalTests.name: testIncidentJournalSurvivesAFreshStoreAndIsSurfacedByAFreshLibrary
additionalTests.pins: Claim (3) — the durable incident journal — end to end across process boundaries. The existing testWholeFileQuarantineWarningSurvivesSubsequentLoads only exercises ONE LocalDropStore instance and never goes through DropLibrary, so nothing pins that the journal actually survives a relaunch or that the user ever sees it. It also pins the two failure classes the current suite ignores entirely: the read-failure incident written at DropStore.swift:98 before the rethrow, and the partial-rows incident at 111.
additionalTests.steps: Arrange: write invalid JSON to a temp URL. Act: store1 = LocalDropStore(fileURL: url); _ = try await store1.loadDrops(...) (quarantines and journals); drop store1 entirely; construct store2 = LocalDropStore(fileURL: url) — a fresh actor with an empty in-memory pendingReadWarning, i.e. the relaunch — and construct library = DropLibrary(localStore: store2, cloudStore: nil, defaults: injectedSuite); await library.refresh(near: nil). Assert: (1) await store2.lastLoadReadWarning() is non-nil and mentions the quarantine file; (2) library.localReadWarning is non-nil after the refresh, so the Sent banner (DropsListScreen.swift:58) actually fires post-relaunch; (3) because the warning is non-nil, a seeded orphan pending id is NOT reaped (DropStore.swift:321) — the safety interlock holds after relaunch, not just in-process; (4) then try await library.add(GeoDrop()) and refresh again: localReadWarning is nil and the .incident sidecar file no longer exists on disk. Repeat the whole arrangement for the partial-rows case (one good row + one type-mismatched row) and for a read failure (make the path a directory so Data(contentsOf:) throws), asserting the journal is written in each case and cleared only by a clean non-empty load.
additionalTests.infrastructure: Existing temporaryFile helper and injected-defaults helper; needs FileManager assertions on the .incident sidecar path and a directory-at-path trick to force a genuine read failure. No new production seams.

additionalTests.name: testEveryFirestoreWriteGoesThroughTheAckedSeam
additionalTests.pins: Claim (4) — "ONE acked-write seam; raw setData outside this file is a review defect". Today that invariant is enforced by a comment in FirestoreAcked.swift only. The omitted copy of this seam is exactly where the PBS-4 silent-write bug survived two rounds (ReactionService), so the guarantee is worth a machine check rather than a reviewer's memory — especially as Wave D adds reaction-read, profile-stat, and memory writes.
additionalTests.steps: Arrange: resolve the source root (SRCROOT injected via the test target's environment, or a path derived from #filePath) and enumerate every .swift file under AugmentMeReality/. Act: scan for the regexes `\.setData\(`, `\.updateData\(`, and `\.addDocument\(`. Assert: the only file with a match is Services/FirestoreAcked.swift; any other hit fails with the offending file:line so the reviewer sees the drift immediately. Complementary runtime half: assert ReactionService.send(_:to:from:) is `throws` and that with no authenticated user it throws DropStoreError.notSignedIn rather than returning silently (ReactionService.swift:682-686 of the diff) — the fast-fail arm the overlay depends on for its .failed state.
additionalTests.infrastructure: A plain XCTestCase using FileManager plus SRCROOT in the test scheme's environment (or #filePath-relative walking). No app state, no Firebase, runs in milliseconds.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and understated. The mechanism is exactly as described: didReact (ReactionSession.swift:47-50) only latches, startWrap moved into reactionDelivered (:53-57), whose sole caller is the success branch at :165-172, which awaits FirestoreAcked.setData. Firestore write completions are documented/known not to fire until the backend commits, so offline the continuation never resumes and never throws — confirmed across three Firebase SDKs (ios-sdk#478, js-sdk#6515, flutterfire#17643). But the reviewer stopped one step short of the real severity. I grepped the whole app for routes into .memory: `startWrap` is the ONLY one (extendSession requires already-wrapping), and reactionFailed() at :60-62 does not call it. So the payoff is gated on a server ACCEPT in every failure mode, not just offline — a rules rejection, a quota error, and the notSignedIn fast-fail in ReactionService.send:38-41 all leave phase == .watching forever with the X button as the only exit. The finding says 'offline'; the defect is 'any non-success'. Also correct that each tap leaks a permanently-parked Task: FirestoreAcked uses a bare withCheckedThrowingContinuation with no cancellation handler, so nothing can ever reclaim it.
solutions.industrialSolution: This is the standard optimistic-UI / delivery-receipt split that iMessage, WhatsApp and Slack all implement, and Firestore ships the exact primitives for it. (1) Local acknowledgment drives lifecycle: Firestore's documented local-vs-server signal is SnapshotMetadata.hasPendingWrites — the write is durably queued in the local cache the instant it is issued, and the docs explicitly tell you to read cache-first rather than wait on the callback. Start the wrap on that (i.e. immediately in didReact), which is a truthful claim: 'we have durably queued this.' (2) Server acknowledgment drives the receipt only: keep `delivery` as .sending → .delivered on ack. (3) Add a bounded deadline at the seam, not the call site: race the ack against Task.sleep in a withThrowingTaskGroup and resolve expiry to a distinct .queued state ('Will send when you're back online') rather than .failed — this is what Firestore.waitForPendingWrites() exists for and how it is used in offline-first apps (it resolves when previously-issued writes, including from a prior app session, are acknowledged by the backend). (4) Make the wait cancellable: wrap the continuation in withTaskCancellationHandler so a superseded or abandoned send is actually reclaimed. (5) Widen the Delivery enum to .sending/.queued/.delivered/.failed and make reactionFailed and a new reactionQueued both start the wrap — the session lifecycle must have no edge that depends on network I/O.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED on mechanism, slightly OVERSTATED on permanence. Every line citation checks out: clearIncident() runs only inside `dropped == 0 && !drops.isEmpty` (DropStore.swift:112-118); lastLoadReadWarning() (:158-164) returns the journaled incident ahead of the transient verdict; the reap is gated on `localReadWarning == nil` (:321); and the quarantine path (:120-133) both empties the library and writes the incident, so the reap is disabled in the same instant the orphan state it fixes is created. reconcileCloud (:418-422) genuinely cannot push those ids because `drops.first(where:)` finds nothing. The round's own test (DropStoreTests.swift:69-87) encodes 'a clean NON-EMPTY library resolves the incident' as intended behavior, so this is design, not slip. The overstatement: it is not immortal. LocalDropStore.save() → loadDrops → persist means creating any single drop produces a clean non-empty load on the next refresh and clears it. So the correct claim is 'persists until the user happens to create another drop' — which the reviewer does concede in one clause but the headline contradicts. Still wrong, still user-visible, and the deadlock with the reap is real for as long as it lasts. The second scenario (healthy empty library + one transient read failure ⇒ permanent banner) is fully confirmed and is the worse of the two, because the transient Data(contentsOf:) failure at :96-99 is journaled durably at :98 even though nothing was destroyed.
solutions.industrialSolution: Separate liveness from safety, which is the standard journaling discipline in any WAL/crash-recovery design (and what SQLite, Core Data and every log-structured store do): the journal records DESTRUCTION, the level records CURRENT READABILITY, and they clear on different events. Concretely: (a) journal only genuinely destructive verdicts — quarantine and skipped rows — and route the transient read failure at :96-99 through pendingReadWarning, not writeIncident; a file you cannot read right now is not a file you have lost. (b) Resolve the incident on a recovery-consistent event, not on a row count: write the incident as a small JSON record {message, quarantinedAt} and clear it when a persist() succeeds with a timestamp after quarantinedAt — 'the store has been successfully written since the damage' is the correct resolution predicate, and it holds for an empty library. (c) Give the reap its own predicate. `localReadWarning == nil` is a UI string, and gating a data-destroying operation on the emptiness of a user-facing string is the category error here. Return a per-load verdict from the store — `enum LoadOutcome { case clean(rowCount: Int), skippedRows(Int), quarantined, unreadable }` — and reap only on .clean. (d) Cache the incident in the actor and re-read only after writeIncident/clearIncident; hitting the disk inside every refresh's warning lookup is needless I/O on the exact path that is already suspected of disk trouble.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED. All four load-bearing claims verified. (1) The tombstone filter moved to the whole merged set (DropStore.swift:314, after the local merge at :274) — verified. (2) The catch-all at :491-499 keeps the tombstone with no expiry, clearPendingDelete has exactly one caller (:487, the success path) — verified by grep. (3) pendingDeleteIDs is durable (:526-534 / :257-258) — verified. (4) The notFound mapping at FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97 is dead code for the never-uploaded case, because under owner-gated rules (`resource.data.ownerUid == request.auth.uid`) a delete of an absent document evaluates `resource` as null, the condition errors, and Firestore returns PERMISSION_DENIED — not NOT_FOUND. That is documented rules semantics: `resource` refers to the requested document, so there is nothing to dereference. Verified. (5) The ghost at :483-484 has ownerUid == nil so the owner backstop at FirebaseDropStore.swift:86 never short-circuits — verified. One important addition the reviewer missed: remove() calls clearPending(drop.id) at :382 BEFORE markPendingDelete at :387, so by the time launchCloudDelete runs, the very fact the correct fix needs ('was this drop ever acked?') has already been destroyed. Any fix must capture that predicate before line 382. The zombie scenario is also confirmed end-to-end: RootView.swift:63 persists a re-received drop to disk and publishes it, and the next refresh strips it at :314 while the row survives on disk — invisible and undeletable.
solutions.industrialSolution: Model the delete as a two-part fact, which is how every replicated store treats tombstones: an INTENT owed to the server (retryable, retirable) and a SUPPRESSION (must outlive the intent). (1) Do not issue a cloud delete you can prove is unnecessary. Capture `let wasNeverAcked = pendingSyncIDs.contains(drop.id) || drop.ownerUid == nil` at the top of remove(), before :382. A never-acked drop cannot have a server document, so the intent is satisfied locally — skip launchCloudDelete entirely and never create a retryable tombstone. This is the cheapest correct fix and it eliminates the dominant trigger. (2) Widen the store seam to match real rules semantics: map FirestoreErrorCode.permissionDenied on a delete to success when the caller declares the document was never acknowledged. Pass the real drop, not a synthesized ghost, so FirebaseDropStore's owner backstop at :86 can also do its job. (3) Give tombstones a lifecycle, as Cassandra/Riak/CRDT stores do with gc_grace_seconds: persist {id, firstAttemptAt, attempts} and after N attempts or T days move the id into a separate durable `suppressedDeleteIDs` set that still feeds the merge suppression but no longer feeds retries or the 'Finishing N deletions…' caption. (4) Clear suppression on deliberate re-acquisition — add()/update() with the same id is an explicit user intent that outranks a stale tombstone, which is exactly how a re-received gift must behave.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and the reviewer's own trigger is far more common than they realised. Code claims all verify: the terminal set is restored uid-blind (:259-260), markTerminal persists a bare id (:514-517), reconcileCloud iterates pendingSyncIDs only and terminal ids were removed from it at :471, and ShareDropSheet.swift:184-188 hard-returns before library.update, so the only surface that reports the problem cannot trigger the retry that clears it. Where I want to strengthen the finding: the reviewer frames uid loss as an exotic keychain reset. It is the ordinary iPhone upgrade. Firebase iOS stores auth state in the keychain under a `...ThisDeviceOnly` accessibility class, and Apple documents that ThisDeviceOnly items do not migrate to a new device via backup — while Apple equally documents that everything in the app's home directory except the bundle, Caches and tmp IS backed up, which includes Library/Application Support/AugmentMeReality/drops.json. So a restore-to-new-device deterministically produces: local rows carrying ownerUid A restored, keychain not restored, fresh anonymous uid B, cloud read (`whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)`) returns empty, and the first edit or share of each restored drop throws ownedByAnotherAccount and marks it terminal, durably, with no recovery path in the app. One narrowing worth recording: FirebaseDropStore.save stamps ownerUid on the cloud copy only (`var stored = drop; stored.ownerUid = uid`), so the terminal verdict bites only drops that round-tripped through a cloud read and were later persisted locally — real, but not literally every drop. The reviewer's 'uid A can legitimately come back' is also weaker than stated for a device migration (ThisDeviceOnly means it will not), though it holds for same-device reinstall and for Sign in with Apple credential linking, which preserves the uid.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two standard moves. (1) Scope a conditional verdict to the condition that produced it. The mismatch is uid-relative (FirebaseDropStore.swift:55-57 compares against the CURRENT uid), so persist it as an id→uid map (`terminalSyncDropOwners: [UUID: String]`) or key the defaults entry by uid. On the auth-ready hook that already calls refresh/reconcile (RootView.swift:155-158), drop every entry whose recorded uid differs from the live uid and move those ids back into pendingSyncIDs for one honest retry. This is ordinary cache-invalidation hygiene: a derived verdict must carry the inputs it was derived from. (2) Ship the actual account-migration path, because this is a known, solved problem class in Firebase apps: Firebase's documented upgrade route is anonymous-account linking (linkWithCredential / Sign in with Apple), which preserves the SAME uid across devices and is the only real fix for the migration scenario — the keychain will never carry it. Until that entitlement exists, at minimum add a reclaim affordance: a 'These drops were made on a previous connection — re-upload them to this account' action that re-stamps ownerUid to the current uid and re-enqueues. (3) Independently, downgrade the ShareDropSheet hard-refusal at :184 to a warning plus an explicit 'Try uploading again' button that calls library.update(sharedDrop) — a terminal state with no user-reachable retry is a dead end, not honesty.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and I would argue the severity is understated for this wave specifically. The SwiftUI behavior is not in dispute: .sheet and .fullScreenCover create separate presentation hierarchies, and an .overlay attached to the presenting view is constrained to that view's tree — it cannot draw above a presented cover. This is well-established and Apple's own developer forums carry the exact question ('How to display a toast view above both main content and FullScreenCover'), with the accepted answers being a separate UIWindow or duplicating the overlay inside the cover. The code matches: the overlay is on the ZStack at RootView.swift:18-22 while camera (:28), create (:35), onboarding (:42) and Memory (:75) are all fullScreenCovers and ReceiveScreen (:55) is a sheet. The receive-flow timing is worse than described — `router.showCamera = true` at :71 executes synchronously right after the Task is created at :61, so the cover is up before `library.update` has even suspended, let alone thrown. Confirmed that lastPersistError has no auto-clear (unlike GeoARSessionManager.showPersistError's 4 s task at :87-96) and is nil'd only by a later successful mutation (:341, :363, :377), so the stale banner genuinely arrives minutes later over an unrelated tab. Also confirmed: the same failure is announced twice — once into arHolder.manager.showPersistError at RootView.swift:65 and once into library.lastPersistError inside update()'s catch at :360. Severity: MEDIUM by data-loss impact is fair, but this is a failure-visibility mechanism that is invisible in the two contexts its own code comment names as the reason it exists. Against a charter of 'make failure visible', that is a charter miss, not a cosmetic one.
solutions.industrialSolution: Presentation-layer errors need a presentation-layer router, not a modifier bolted to one node. Two accepted patterns: (a) the UIWindow overlay — host the banner in a short-lived UIWindow at a windowLevel above .normal, which is the only approach that reliably draws above sheets, covers and system alerts; this is the standard production toast implementation on iOS. (b) The composable-modifier approach — define `func failureBanner(_ text: Binding<String?>) -> some View` once and apply it to the ZStack AND to each cover's root, so whichever context is frontmost owns the announcement. (b) is the smaller change and adequate here. Independently, fix the double-announce with a single-delivery discipline: give lastPersistError an identity (UUID + timestamp) and mark it consumed when any context-local channel (CreateWizard.placeError, manager.persistErrorText) has already surfaced it, so one failure is announced exactly once, in the context where it happened. Auto-expire it as well; an undismissed banner with no referent is worse than none.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED. Verified against the source: showPersistError is called from inside makeHolder (GeoARSessionManager.swift:1517-1520); makeHolder is invoked from the room test (:511), the pedestrian placement else-branch (:1454) and tickTransit's per-tick loop (:1959), each guarded only by `placedHolders[id] == nil`; holders are torn down in the cleanup loops immediately after each placement pass, so any drop leaving the eligible set and returning re-enters the factory. showPersistError (:87-96) overwrites the single persistErrorText slot and cancels/restarts the 4 s clear task, and ARScreen.swift:407 renders that one slot, which is also written by the slider-commit failures at :1640 and :1813 and by RootView.swift:65. The clobbering scenario is exactly right, and the framing is the sharpest thing in this finding: this is the shared last-writer-wins slot that round 4 spent DropLibrary's entire redesign eliminating, reintroduced one file over. One conditional: 'a live decode failure now fires twice' holds only when the decode fails while the manager is alive AND a holder is subsequently built — DropEntityFactory.onAssetLoaded is assigned at :321-325, so a launch-preload failure that predates the manager fires only through makeHolder, which is the case the round-4 comment says it added this for. So the duplicate is real but not universal.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two separate rules, both standard. (1) A factory does not narrate. Announcement is a side effect on shared UI state; putting it inside a per-tick entity constructor makes announcement frequency a function of render topology, which is uncontrollable. Compute the failed-asset set once per placement pass at the call sites (:1454, :1959) — you already have the drop set there — and route it through its own `@Published private(set) var assetErrorText: String?` rendered as a distinct line near ARScreen.swift:407. (2) Notifications need identity and coalescing, which is precisely what iOS's own notification model formalizes: an identifier so a repeat replaces rather than re-fires, and a thread so related items group. Mirror it: keep `announcedFailedAssets: Set<String>` and guard on `insert(name).inserted` so each asset is announced once per session, and aggregate co-occurring failures ('2 drops' 3D models couldn't be loaded') instead of letting the last writer win. (3) Give persistErrorText a severity so a data-loss message cannot be evicted by a cosmetic one inside its display window — a two-slot model (dataLoss / advisory) is simpler and more honest than a priority queue here.
