(4) Skip the announcement when roomDrops[drop.id] != nil so the room test never names a drop the user did not create.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same defect as sync-3/arui-1/flows-1, and this write-up isolates the cleanest trigger. Verified: launchCloudDelete's catch-all (:491-499) only increments deleteAttempts and logs; clearPendingDelete has exactly one caller (:487); deleteAttempts is in-memory (:235) so the `< 3` bound at :423-424 resets every launch while pendingDeleteIDs persists (:528/:533); ProfileScreen.swift:99-105 sits ahead of the Synced branch at :106-113. The notSignedIn scenario is the sharpest form of the trigger and it is correct: FirebaseDropStore.save throws notSignedIn at :45-47 BEFORE any Firestore write is staged, so no document is ever created even in the local cache, and the later delete is aimed at a document that has never existed in any tier. One correction to the mechanics worth recording: while offline, the delete does not even reach the permission-denied arm — `try await ...delete()` is the async bridge over the completion-handler API and hangs indefinitely without resolving (documented across the JS, iOS and Flutter SDKs), so the parked deleteTask leaves deleteTasks[id] non-nil, which makes reconcileCloud skip that id for the rest of the session. The bounded-retry budget therefore does not even spend offline; it spends on the first online launch and then burns three writes per launch forever. Net: the finding's conclusion is right and its retry-cost arithmetic is if anything conservative.
solutions.industrialSolution: See sync-3 for the tombstone lifecycle; the additions this finding earns are: (1) Make the retry budget durable and per-install, not per-session — persist {attempts, firstAttemptAt} alongside the id, exactly as any at-least-once delivery outbox does. An unbounded-retry-with-in-memory-counter is the classic accidental-DDoS-on-your-own-backend pattern, and here it is aimed at writes that are guaranteed to be refused. (2) Split the durable set in two — `pendingDeleteIDs` (in flight, rendered as work) and `suppressedDeleteIDs` (retired, feeds merge suppression only) — and publish `deletesInFlight` for ProfileScreen.swift:99 so the status ladder cannot be jammed by retired work. (3) Move the whole ladder out of the view: ProfileScreen's if/else chain is an implicit precedence order encoded in a view builder. Compute `enum SyncStatus { connecting, terminal(Int), readError, uploading(Int), synced }` on DropLibrary with an explicit, unit-testable precedence, and let the view render it. Deletes should not appear in a user-facing status ladder at all — the user has expressed no interest in a deletion's server-side completion, and blocking 'Synced' on it is a category error. (4) Apply exponential backoff with jitter to whatever retries remain, per Google's own guidance for its APIs.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and Case B is the strongest single observation in the whole set. Case A is the sync-1 defect. Case B — the late ack landing on a different session — is verified line by line: reactionDelivered() (:53-57) takes no drop id and no generation; the overlay Task at :165-172 captures the shared ReactionSession EnvironmentObject (RootView.swift:13/24) with no identity check and no cancellation; startWatching (:29-36) resets sentEmoji/delivery/phase but holds no handle on the in-flight send; endSession (:86-92) does not reset delivery at all. So a parked continuation that resumes minutes later calls startWrap on whatever session is current, and because reactionDelivered guards only on `case .watching = phase`, the new session is precisely the state that qualifies. The user gets a 15 s countdown appearing from nowhere with no pill (sentEmoji is nil), then a forced transition to .memory with memorySnapshot nil and myReaction nil. I verified there is no other route into .memory, so this is not merely a cosmetic state flip — it terminates a live AR moment. Also confirmed: Task.cancel() would not help even if a handle existed, because FirestoreAcked's withCheckedThrowingContinuation has no cancellation handler and cannot be resumed by cancellation.
solutions.industrialSolution: Address the message to its session, and bound the wait — the two halves of standard async-completion hygiene. (1) Identity: this is the same generation-token discipline DropStore already applies at :443/:455/:461/:470/:475, and the fix is to apply it consistently rather than invent a new one. Mint a token in didReact (or key on the watched drop's id, which is more legible), pass it through the Task, and make reactionDelivered(token:)/reactionFailed(token:) no-op on a mismatch. startWatching and endSession mint a fresh token so in-flight sends are orphaned by construction. (2) Ownership: store the send Task on the session and cancel it in startWatching/endSession — but make cancellation MEAN something by wrapping the continuation in withTaskCancellationHandler at the FirestoreAcked seam, otherwise cancel() only detaches the Swift task while the Firestore continuation stays parked and the memory stays live. (3) Bound: race the send against Task.sleep in a withThrowingTaskGroup (8-10 s) and treat expiry as .queued, so no session lifecycle edge is reachable only via network I/O. (4) Structural: an app-wide @EnvironmentObject mutated from an unstructured detached Task is the root shape here. Scoping the send to a `.task(id: drop.id)` on the overlay would give SwiftUI-managed cancellation on identity change for free and remove an entire class of these.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED. AccountService.swift:78-93 is verbatim the round-3 loop — I diffed it against the described shape and only the write seam changed (a local acked-write helper replaced by FirestoreAcked.setData at :80). There is no isSeeding flag, no seedTask handle, and the `self.profile == nil` guard at :58-64 is evaluated once per listener event and never re-evaluated inside the retry loop or after the 1.5 s/3 s backoff sleeps at :90. FirestoreAcked defaults to merge: true (FirestoreAcked.swift:19), so the starter's displayName and handle do overwrite server-side fields, and :83 then republishes the starter locally over whatever the user typed. The listener is registered with includeMetadataChanges: true (:46), which by design produces multiple events, so overlapping seed loops are expected rather than exotic. updateProfile (:101-123) publishes optimistically and fires its own unawaited acked write, so the interleaving is a genuine last-writer race with no ordering guarantee. The failure narrative — user names themselves during the backoff window, attempt 2 destroys it on screen and on the server with no error — is exactly what this code does. HIGH is the right severity; it is not a ship blocker only because the damage is user-recoverable by re-editing.
solutions.industrialSolution: Make 'create if absent' a real precondition rather than a client-side check, then make the client single-flight. (1) Server-side, this is what Firestore's granular write methods are for: rules distinguish `create` (writing a document that does not exist) from `update` (writing one that does). Grant the seed path `allow create: if request.auth.uid == uid` only, and issue the seed as setData(merge: false). An attempt that races a real profile is then rejected by the backend as an update, not silently merged — the guarantee lives where concurrency actually resolves. Equivalently, use a Firestore transaction that reads the doc and aborts if it exists; transactions retry on contention and are the documented primitive for read-then-conditional-write. (2) Client-side, add `private var seedTask: Task<Void, Never>?` and a single-flight entry point that returns immediately if it is non-nil, clearing in a defer. (3) Re-check the invariant at every attempt, not once at entry: `guard profile == nil else { return }` at the top of each iteration AND immediately after the backoff sleep — a guard evaluated before a suspension point is not a guard. (4) Never publish `profile = starter` if profile became non-nil while the write was in flight; and give updateProfile the same generation token so a slow seed cannot republish over a newer edit.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, exactly as specified. The catch branch is: guard at :279 (before the await), then `localReadWarning = await localStore.lastLoadReadWarning()` at :281 assigning across a suspension point with no re-check, then a second unguarded write at :283-285. The success path immediately below at :288-291 does it correctly — binds to a local, re-checks, then publishes — so the two paths genuinely disagree, which makes this a slip rather than a considered trade-off, and the class doc at :196-198 asserts the discipline that :281 breaks. The await is real work: lastLoadReadWarning() does Data(contentsOf:) on the incident file (:159) serialized on the LocalDropStore actor behind any queued save/persist, so the suspension window is not theoretical — a slider commit's persist is exactly what sits in that queue. Test-coverage claim also verified: FlakyLocalStore (DropStoreTests.swift:506) is a bare `actor ... : DropStore` and not a LocalDropStore, so `local as? LocalDropStore` fails and testFailingLocalReadNeitherHidesTheFailureNorClearsState (:352-368) only ever exercises the hardcoded fallback at :284. The escalation is right too: because :321 gates the reap on this field, a stale non-nil write suppresses the next pass's reap as well.
solutions.industrialSolution: Two standard fixes, one for the bug and one for the reason it was invisible. (1) Sequence-number guarding must be mechanical, not remembered. Mirror the success path — bind the awaited value to a local, re-check the generation, then publish — and then remove the possibility of forgetting: funnel every publish through a single `private func publish(generation:_ body:)` helper that re-checks and no-ops on mismatch, so a bare assignment to published state after an await becomes impossible by construction rather than by convention. This is the same discipline as the epoch/fencing-token pattern in distributed systems: the token is checked at the write, not at the read. (2) Stop keying behavior on a concrete type. `local as? LocalDropStore` makes an entire production branch unreachable from every test double, which is why the round-4 test passes while asserting nothing about the defect. Hoist it into a protocol — `protocol ReadWarningReporting { func lastLoadReadWarning() async -> String? }` with the DropStore doubles adopting it — and have the diagnostic ride the seam rather than the implementation. Better still, return the load verdict from loadDrops itself (see sync-2) so there is no second call and no second await to guard.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED on mechanism, OVERSTATED on permanence — same correction as sync-2. The deadlock is real and correctly traced: clearIncident only inside `dropped == 0 && !drops.isEmpty` (:112-118), the file-absent early return deliberately does not clear (:85-91), the quarantine writes the incident including the raw filename at :131, lastLoadReadWarning ranks the incident first (:158-164), and the reap requires it to be nil (:321). Both round-4 mechanisms do disable each other. But 'permanent' is wrong: LocalDropStore.save() persists then the next load is clean-and-non-empty, so creating any drop clears it. The claim should be 'until the user creates another drop', which is a genuine defect but a bounded one. Fully confirmed and worth keeping: the raw quarantine filename ('drops.json.corrupt-1755284431') is leaked into user-facing copy at :131 and rendered as-is by DropsListScreen.swift:58-60; there is no dismiss affordance, in contrast to the OK button round 4 gave lastPersistError at RootView.swift:132; and lastLoadReadWarning() re-reads the incident file from disk on every call. Minor precision note: it is called once per refresh, not once or twice — the catch branch (:281) and the success branch (:289) are mutually exclusive.
solutions.industrialSolution: Same core fix as sync-2 — resolve on 'a successful persist has occurred since the quarantine', not on row count, and give the reap its own per-load verdict. Beyond that, three product-grade conventions: (1) Every persistent user-facing warning needs an acknowledgement path. A banner the user cannot dismiss and cannot act on is a permanent accusation; match lastPersistError's OK button, and record the acknowledgement in the incident record so it does not return on relaunch while remaining in the log. (2) Diagnostic identifiers do not belong in user copy — Apple's guidance is that error messages should be actionable and understandable, with technical detail in logs. Keep the quarantine filename in os_log (it is already logged at :129) and tell the user only what they can act on. Retaining the corrupt file for support is right; naming it at them is not. (3) Cache the incident in the actor, invalidated on writeIncident/clearIncident, so the diagnostic path stops doing synchronous disk I/O inside the refresh that is already suspected of disk trouble.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same defect as sync-6/arui-6. All mechanics verified: the announcement is inside makeHolder (:1513-1520); holders are created only when placedHolders[id] == nil and torn down in the cleanup loop whenever a drop leaves the tick's radius-filtered set, so range boundary jitter genuinely cycles them; showPersistError (:87-96) is a single last-writer-wins slot that cancels and recreates its 4 s clear Task on every call; and RootView.swift:65 now routes the received-drop save failure — a genuine data-loss message — into that same slot. The clobbering direction the reviewer highlights (cosmetic asset news evicting a data-loss warning within a frame) is the one that matters and it is correct. I would rate this MEDIUM rather than LOW, for that reason: the severity is not the strobing, it is that the only in-AR channel for 'this drop may disappear after this session' can be silently overwritten by a decorative notice. The added observation about republishing @Published state during frame updates is also fair — SwiftUI invalidation driven from a per-frame render loop is a real cost, though secondary here.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-6: hoist the announcement out of the per-frame factory to the drop-set-change boundary, give asset failures their own published slot distinct from persistErrorText, and de-duplicate with an `announcedFailedAssets: Set<String>` guarded on `insert(name).inserted`. The specific addition this finding earns is the priority point: implement persistErrorText as two slots rather than one — a `dataLossText` that is sticky until acknowledged and an `advisoryText` that auto-clears — so severity, not arrival order, decides what the user reads. Last-writer-wins is only acceptable when all writers carry equal consequence, which stopped being true the moment RootView started routing a persistence failure into it. Additionally, do not publish @Published changes from the render tick: coalesce announcements to the placement-pass boundary so SwiftUI invalidation is bounded by drop-set changes rather than frame rate.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — the fourth independent statement of the tombstone defect, and the one that best articulates the second-order consequence. Everything verifies: the `< 3` bound at :423-426, the keep-forever catch at :491-499, clearPendingDelete's single success-path caller at :487, the durable key written at :526-529/:536-538, the whole-merged-set suppression at :314, and the ProfileScreen ordering at :99-113 that puts 'Finishing N deletions…' above 'Synced'. The characterisation of the trigger as common rather than edge is correct: creating a drop in airplane mode or before anonymous auth resolves is the app's stated field scenario, and under owner-gated rules a delete aimed at a document that was never written returns permission-denied because `resource` is null — so the notFound mapping at FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97 is dead code for precisely that path. The framing 'a permanent id-level blacklist that silently deletes any drop that legitimately reappears under that id' is the most accurate one-line summary of the risk across all four write-ups, because it names the silent-data-loss consequence rather than the cosmetic one. The proposed fix (split in-flight from suppressed, publish deletesInFlight, treat never-acked permission-denied as satisfied, clear suppression on re-add) is correct and is the same shape I would recommend.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-3/concurrency-1. The one thing to add at this seam specifically: the repository contains no firestore.rules and web/firebase.json declares hosting only — so the entire client-side error-mapping contract (notFound vs permissionDenied on delete) is written against rules that are neither version-controlled nor tested here. That is the actual root cause of this finding surviving a round of review: nobody could check the premise. The industrial standard is rules-as-code committed alongside the app plus rules unit tests run in CI against the Firestore emulator using @firebase/rules-unit-testing, which lets you assert exactly this case — 'delete of a nonexistent document by an authenticated non-owner returns permission-denied' — as an executable test rather than a comment. Add the rules file, add a rules test for each error the client maps, and the mapping stops being folklore.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — the same defect as sync-1/concurrency-2/flows-3, correctly traced through the whole chain (didReact :47-50 → reactionDelivered :53-57 → the Task at :165-172 → ReactionService.send :46-51 → FirestoreAcked.setData :19-33 → withCheckedThrowingContinuation on setData's completion). The platform premise is right and independently well-evidenced across the Firebase SDKs. The observation that this is a regression introduced by the honesty fix, in the field condition an outdoor AR app spends most of its time in, is the correct framing for triage. The one thing I would add, which none of the four write-ups states outright: since startWrap is the only route into .memory anywhere in the app and reactionFailed does not call it, the Memory screen is unreachable on ANY delivery failure — the notSignedIn fast-fail in ReactionService.send:38-41 strands the session while fully online, and so does a rules rejection. Framing it as an offline bug understates it and risks a fix that only handles the offline path.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-1. The specific point this write-up gets right and should drive the fix: 'phase must never be able to remain .watching indefinitely because of a network condition' — generalise that to 'because of any delivery outcome'. The invariant to encode and test is that every terminal outcome of the send (delivered, rejected, queued, timed out, cancelled) leads to a wrap. Write it as a state-machine test over Delivery × Phase asserting that .watching is not reachable as a fixed point from any send result — that is a five-line test and it is the one that would have caught this in round 4, where the existing suite has no ReactionSession coverage at all.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED in its core claim, with the mechanism misidentified — and the correction makes the finding stronger, not weaker. Core claim: `localReadWarning == nil` does not prove a successful read, so gating a destructive reap on it is unsound. That is right, and the round-4 test at DropStoreTests.swift:397-410 does encode the unsound invariant — it seeds a ghost pending id, refreshes over a URL that was never written, and asserts the reap fired, i.e. it asserts that a load of a nonexistent file is proof the drop is gone. Where the finding is weak is the trigger. 'The container is relocated / the store file otherwise vanishes' is not a realistic iOS scenario: Application Support is not purgeable (only Caches and tmp are), App Offloading preserves data, the path is resolved at runtime so container UUID changes are invisible, `Data.write(options: .atomic)` writes to a temp file and renames so a crash leaves the original intact, and a restore-to-new-device restores Application Support. The realistic trigger is inside the code: the quarantine branch sets `pendingReadWarning = nil` (:130) and depends entirely on `writeIncident` (:148-150) which uses `try?` and silently swallows failure. On a full disk — the exact condition that produces a truncated drops.json — the incident write fails, lastLoadReadWarning() returns nil after a load that just quarantined the library, and refresh() reaps the entire outbox. Same conclusion, a trigger that actually occurs, and it explains why the guard was believed sufficient.
solutions.industrialSolution: Return the verdict, do not infer it from a side channel. Have loadDrops return `(drops, LoadOutcome)` where LoadOutcome is `.clean(rowCount:)`, `.skippedRows(Int)`, `.quarantined`, `.absent`, `.unreadable` — an explicit sum type that cannot be forged by a failed disk write — and gate the reap at :321 on `.clean` only, never on `.absent`. This is the standard distinction between 'read a real file cleanly' and 'there was nothing to read' that any recovery-capable store maintains; conflating them is how the round-2 C1 bug returns. Two supporting moves: (1) stop using `try?` on the journal write — if the incident cannot be recorded, that failure must itself degrade the verdict (treat 'quarantined but could not journal' as the most severe state, not the cleanest). (2) Fix the test to match the invariant: write a real empty `[]` store file in the arrange step, so it asserts 'a clean load of an existing empty store reaps orphans' rather than 'the absence of a file is proof of deletion'. Reaping is a destructive operation on the user's outbox; the predicate guarding it deserves the same rigor as the predicate guarding a delete.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — identical to concurrency-4 and flows-6, and this version adds the most useful detail: it correctly notes that BOTH sites (:280 and :288) reach the warning through an `as? LocalDropStore` downcast, so the entire branch is unreachable from FlakyLocalStore and the round-4 test that claims to cover it (:352-368) falls through to the hardcoded fallback string at :284 and asserts nothing about the defect. I verified FlakyLocalStore at DropStoreTests.swift:506 — it is a bare `actor ... : DropStore` with no relationship to LocalDropStore, so the downcast fails and the awaited branch never executes in any test. The compounding claim is also right: :321 gates the orphan reap on this exact field, so a stale non-nil write suppresses the next pass's reap. Severity MEDIUM is fair — the user-visible damage is a false banner over a healthy list, and the reap suppression is bounded by the next successful refresh.
solutions.industrialSolution: As concurrency-4: mirror the success path, then make the discipline structural via a single generation-checked publish helper so a bare post-await assignment to published state cannot compile past review. The testability point deserves equal weight and is the more valuable half: replace the concrete downcasts with a protocol the doubles can adopt (`ReadWarningReporting`, or better, fold the verdict into loadDrops' return per arui-3), because a production branch that no test double can enter is not merely untested — it is structurally untestable, and round 4 shipped a test whose name claims coverage it does not have. That gap is more dangerous than the bug: it converts an open defect into a closed one in the review record.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — third statement of the :281 defect, consistent with concurrency-4 and flows-6, and the failure narrative here is the most concrete (refresh A suspends in the catch, the auth-ready task at RootView.swift:155-158 fires refresh B which succeeds and clears the warning, A resumes and overwrites). I verified that RootView.swift:155-158 is a real independent refresh trigger keyed on account.uid, so the interleaving is not hypothetical — auth resolution during a transient data-protection window is precisely when both would run. The claim that the banner 'cannot be dismissed' is correct: DropsListScreen.swift:58-62 renders localReadWarning as a plain Label with no dismiss control, unlike lastPersistError which got an OK button in round 4.
solutions.industrialSolution: As concurrency-4/arui-4. The additional point specific to this write-up: it correctly observes that the two paths in the same function disagree about the discipline, which is the signal that the invariant lives in a comment (:196-198) rather than in the type system. Move it into the type system — a `Publisher(generation:)` value that owns the mutating access, or a private `withCurrentGeneration { }` wrapper — so the compiler enforces what the doc comment currently asks reviewers to notice. Every mechanically-enforceable invariant that is documented instead of enforced will be violated in a later round; this file now has three reviewers finding the same one, which is the evidence.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and it is the most complete of the three makeHolder write-ups — it is the only one to catch the N-collapses-to-1 problem and the room-test misfire. Verified: multiple failed drops placed in the same tick produce N showPersistError calls into one slot, so only the last title survives; the parallel subscriber at :321-325 announces the same class of failure with different wording ('A 3D model couldn't be loaded'), so one broken USDZ can yield two differently-worded toasts; and placeRoomDrop (:492-511) does call makeHolder for a synthetic drop with createdBy 'Room test' and an assetName, so an animated room test can name a drop the user never created. The 4 s window resetting on every re-fire is correct and is what turns a notice into a permanent fixture. The one place I would push back on the framing: the finding calls the announcement 'noise' and the consequence 'blocks the statusText line'. The more serious consequence, which concurrency-6 names and this one under-weights, is that the same slot carries 'Couldn't save this drop — it may disappear after this session' from RootView.swift:65, so the noise does not merely crowd out guidance, it evicts a data-loss warning.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-6/concurrency-6: hoist out of the factory, dedupe per asset per session via `insert(name).inserted`, aggregate co-occurring failures into one message, unify wording with the :324 subscriber so one failure yields exactly one notice, and skip entirely when roomDrops[drop.id] != nil. Add the severity split (dataLoss vs advisory) so eviction cannot go the wrong way. The general principle: a user-facing announcement needs an identity, a coalescing policy and a severity — the same three properties iOS requires of a UNNotificationRequest (identifier, threadIdentifier, interruptionLevel). A raw String slot written from a render loop has none of them, which is why three independent reviewers found three different symptoms of one design choice.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — the fourth statement of the tombstone defect. Its distinctive contribution is the unbounded-growth argument (pendingDeleteDropIDs grows monotonically with every offline-create-then-delete over the install's lifetime, and each launch spends three denied writes per entry), which is correct given that deleteAttempts is in-memory at :235 while the id set is durable at :526-533. The claim that round 3 cleared the tombstone here and round 4 removed the clear without adding a retirement path matches the comment at :492-496, which explicitly documents keeping it as intentional. So this is a deliberate design decision with an unconsidered consequence, not an oversight — worth recording, because the fix must preserve the intent (suppression) while discarding the accident (unretirable in-flight state). The second consequence — a legitimately re-added drop being stripped at :314 while surviving on disk — is the same silent-data-loss case arui-1 names and is the strongest reason to treat this family as a blocker rather than a polish item.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-3/concurrency-1/arui-1. The synthesis across all four write-ups: the design conflated two facts that have different lifetimes and different audiences. 'The server still owes me a delete' is retryable, bounded, and is NOT user-facing work (the user considers the drop deleted the moment the local delete succeeded). 'Do not resurrect this id' is durable, unbounded in time, and must be revocable by an explicit user re-acquisition. Split them into `pendingDeleteIDs` (bounded, durable attempt count, feeds retries only) and `suppressedDeleteIDs` (durable, feeds :314 only, cleared by add()/update() of the same id). Then remove deletions from the ProfileScreen status ladder entirely — computing 'Synced' over a set the user has no interest in and cannot act on is what turns a background retry into a permanent product defect. Pair with the never-acked short-circuit in remove() (capture the predicate before clearPending at :382) and the permissionDenied mapping at the store seam, and this family closes with one coherent change.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, and it is the sharpest finding in the set that no other reviewer duplicates. enqueueCloudSync clears the durable terminal marker at :442 BEFORE the write is issued; clearTerminal (:519-524) also wipes syncFailureReasons and rewrites the persisted array, so the loss survives relaunch; and the success path already clears terminal after the ack at :463, which makes the enqueue-time clear redundant for the good case and purely destructive for the bad one. That asymmetry is the proof it is a bug rather than a trade-off. The trigger is routine — GeoARSessionManager.swift:1636/1813 calls library.update on a slider commit — and offline the write suspends indefinitely (platform fact, verified), so no arm of performCloudSync ever runs and nothing restores the verdict. The downstream consequence is exactly right and is the worst outcome in the whole review: with terminal cleared, ShareDropSheet's guard at :184 stops blocking, the coral warning at :135-143 is replaced by the reassuring gold caption at :144-150, and the user hands a friend a permanently dead magic link — re-arming precisely the failure flows-3 and the terminal machinery were built to prevent. Note also the direct conflict with sync-4, which complains that this clear path is unreachable from the share surface: both reviewers are describing the same design error from opposite ends.
solutions.industrialSolution: Delete the clearTerminal call at :442. A retry is not evidence; only a server response is, and that is already handled at :463 (success) and :467-473 (re-mark). This is the elementary rule that a verdict may be revoked only by the authority that issued it — the client cannot un-know a server refusal by intending to try again. If the UI needs to show that a retry is in flight, add a separate transient `retryingIDs: Set<UUID>` rendered BELOW terminal in the precedence order, so terminal keeps outranking 'Uploading' and 'Synced' in Profile, Sent and ShareDropSheet until the server actually accepts. Combined with sync-4's fix (revalidate terminal against the uid that produced it on auth-ready) this resolves both findings coherently: the verdict is scoped to its cause, revoked only by its cause disappearing or by a server ack, and a retry is visible without being mistaken for a result. Add the regression test the round lacks: mark a drop terminal, go offline, call update(), assert terminalSyncFailureIDs still contains the id and ShareDropSheet's guard still fires.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same defect as sync-1/concurrency-2/arui-2. Distinctive and correct contribution: it identifies that deliveryText (:202-208) renders 'Sending to X…' indefinitely and therefore the 'tap an emoji to retry' affordance at :206 is never shown, so the honesty fix removed the user's only recovery path along with the payoff. Also correct that Firebase auth being warm (anonymous uid in keychain, verified as documented behavior) means send does NOT fast-fail on notSignedIn in the field scenario, so the write stages locally and parks — i.e. the most likely offline path is the hanging one, not the throwing one. The recommended fix is the right one and matches my own: restore the wrap on didReact, keep 'Sent' gated on the ack, add a bounded timeout with a .queued state. The closing line — 'the wrap countdown and the Memory screen must never depend on network I/O' — is the correct invariant to encode.
solutions.industrialSolution: As sync-1. What this write-up adds operationally: the copy for the timeout state matters as much as the state machine. 'Will send when you're back online' is a true statement about Firestore's local write queue — the write IS durably queued in the local cache and will be flushed on reconnect (including across app restarts, which is why waitForPendingWrites is documented to cover writes from a previous session). So the .queued state is not a euphemism for failure; it is the accurate description, and it is the only one of the four possible copies that is both honest and non-alarming. Reserve 'Couldn't send' for an actual server rejection. That mapping — queued vs rejected, not offline vs online — is the industry-standard messaging split and it is what makes the honesty fix compatible with the product loop instead of destructive to it.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — same as concurrency-2 Case B, and this framing ('the completion is applied to whatever drop the shared session is watching when it finally returns') is the clearest one-line statement of it. Verified: the Task at :165-172 captures the drop only as a send argument, the callbacks carry no identity, session is the app-wide @EnvironmentObject (RootView.swift:13/24), startWatching (:29-36) holds no handle on the in-flight task, and reactionDelivered calls startWrap whenever phase is .watching regardless of which drop that phase belongs to. The consequence is correctly identified as worse than a wrong label: because startWrap is the only route into .memory, the orphaned ack terminates a live AR session for drop B and presents MemoryScreen with myReaction nil and memorySnapshot nil. The mirror case (A's rejection painting 'Couldn't send' over B's delivered reaction) is equally real. Correct that round 4 created this exposure by converting a fire-and-forget send into a completion that mutates shared session state — the previous shape had no state to corrupt.
solutions.industrialSolution: Identity-address the completion and bound the task's lifetime to the session's. Concretely: reactionDelivered(for: UUID)/reactionFailed(for: UUID) that no-op when session.drop?.id != id; store the send Task on the session and cancel it in startWatching and endSession; and make cancellation effective by wrapping the continuation at the FirestoreAcked seam in withTaskCancellationHandler, because Task.cancel() on a task parked in a bare withCheckedThrowingContinuation detaches the Swift task but leaves the continuation live — so without that, cancellation is decorative. The structural improvement worth taking: move the send from an unstructured `Task { }` inside a Button action to a `.task(id:)` scoped to the watched drop, which gives SwiftUI-managed cancellation on identity change and eliminates this class of orphan by construction rather than by discipline.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED, every detail. The reap at :321-327 covers pendingSyncIDs only; terminalSyncFailureIDs is restored at :259-260 and its only clearers are remove() (:383, which requires a row to swipe), a successful cloud save (:463, impossible by definition for a terminal drop) and enqueueCloudSync (:442, which is flows-2's separate bug). So a terminal id whose row is gone is permanently uncounterable. The quarantine scenario is exactly the one that produces it, and it composes with sync-2/concurrency-5: the same quarantine that empties the library also freezes the incident, so the user gets 'No drops yet' under an orange '3 drops can't sync' under an undismissable corruption banner, with nothing to tap. I also verified the small precise catch at DropsListScreen.swift:66-70: the vertical padding condition tests lastSyncError, lastPersistError and localReadWarning but omits terminalSyncFailureIDs, so when the terminal banner is the only one shown it renders with zero vertical padding. That is a real, trivially fixable rendering bug and it is a good sign of the review's thoroughness. The unattributable-count criticism is the most product-relevant part: an aggregate 'N drops can't sync' with no per-row indicator gives the user a problem without a referent, which is exactly the failure mode the wave's charter exists to eliminate.
solutions.industrialSolution: Three moves. (1) Apply the same orphan-reap rule to terminal ids that round 4 added for pending — after a genuinely clean load (per arui-3's LoadOutcome, not the banner string), drop any terminal id with no corresponding row. Any durable id set that references rows needs a referential-integrity sweep; the round added one and stopped at the first set. (2) Make the state per-row before it is aggregate: render an xmark.icloud badge on DropRow when library.terminalSyncFailureIDs.contains(drop.id), so the banner's count is verifiable by looking at the list. A count without identification is not actionable information, and Apple's guidance on error presentation is that a message should tell the user what happened and what they can do about it. (3) Add terminalSyncFailureIDs to the padding condition at :68. And once the count is attributable, the per-row surface is the natural home for sync-4's 'try uploading again' affordance.

solutions.verdictOnFinding: CONFIRMED — third independent statement of the :281 defect, and the one that documents the discipline gap most precisely by enumerating the compliant sites (:273, :290, :296, :305, :307) against the one non-compliant site. I verified that enumeration: every other await in refresh() either re-checks the generation before publishing or binds to a local first, and :281 alone assigns the awaited value straight into @Published state, with :283-285 compounding it by writing a second time on the same unguarded path. The failure narrative (refresh A suspends on lastLoadReadWarning; the user creates a drop, which bumps the generation and triggers refresh B; B loads cleanly and clears the warning; A resumes and stamps its stale value) is accurate — add() does bump refreshGeneration at :334. Correctly notes nothing recomputes the banner until the next refresh, so the false 'your library is unreadable' sits above a correct fully-populated list for an unbounded period. The recommendation to extract the diagnostic behind a protocol rather than the `as? LocalDropStore` cast is the same conclusion concurrency-4 and arui-4 reach independently, which is a strong signal it is the right structural fix.
solutions.industrialSolution: As concurrency-4/arui-4/arui-5. Since three reviewers found this same line independently, treat the remedy as structural rather than local: (1) fix :281 and :283 to mirror :288-291; (2) funnel all published-state writes in refresh() through one generation-checked helper so the pattern cannot be broken by a future edit; (3) replace the concrete downcast with a protocol (or fold the verdict into loadDrops' return type, which removes the second await entirely and is the better end state); (4) add the regression test that round 4's version could not express — with the protocol in place, a double can park inside lastLoadReadWarning while a second refresh completes, and the test asserts the stale warning is never published. The general lesson for the round: an invariant asserted in a class doc comment (:196-198) and enforced by reviewer attention will be violated; the same invariant expressed as a single choke-point function is enforced by the compiler.

crossCutting: ROOT CAUSE OF THE ROUND, unnamed by any reviewer: FirestoreAcked is an unbounded, uncancellable suspension point, and round 4 put every write in the app behind it. FirestoreAcked.setData (:20-34) is a bare withCheckedThrowingContinuation with no timeout and no withTaskCancellationHandler. Three consequences no reviewer traced: (a) DropStore's syncTasks[id]?.cancel() at :445 is decorative — cancelling a task parked in a non-cancellation-aware continuation detaches the Swift task but leaves the continuation live forever, so every superseded offline write leaks a permanently-suspended task; (b) the `defer` at :456-458 never runs for a parked task, so syncTasks[id] stays non-nil and reconcileCloud's `where syncTasks[id] == nil` guard silently blocks all future retries for that id for the rest of the session; (c) the same applies to launchCloudDelete, so the 3-attempt budget does not even spend while offline. Every finding in the sync-1/concurrency-2/arui-2/flows-3 family and half of flows-2 and flows-4 are downstream of this one seam. The file's own doc comment names the hazard ('callers own that policy... UI paths must not await this inline') and then ships a UI path that awaits it inline — the seam documented its danger instead of eliminating it.

THE ROUND INVERTED ITS OWN CHARTER IN THE PRODUCT LOOP. Wave C's charter is 'make failure visible'. In the sync surfaces round 4 delivered that well — per-drop state replacing shared last-writer-wins slots, one acked-write seam, durable terminal verdicts, 'Synced' as a computation. But in the reaction path it made failure TERMINAL rather than visible: startWrap is the only route into .memory anywhere in the app (grep-verified), and neither reactionFailed nor any timeout calls it, so every non-success delivery outcome — offline, rules rejection, notSignedIn — permanently strands the session. Making a truth-claim honest by gating a UI lifecycle on it is the wrong lever; the correct pattern separates the RITUAL (local, immediate, always progresses) from the RECEIPT (server-gated, honest, may be pending forever). Round 4 fused them.

THE SAME DESIGN ERROR APPEARS IN THREE PLACES: a verdict is conflated with the intent to retry it. flows-2: enqueueCloudSync clears the durable terminal marker at :442 before the write is issued, so intending a retry revokes a server refusal. sync-4: the only path that clears terminal is that same enqueue, and it is unreachable from ShareDropSheet, the one surface that reports the problem. concurrency-1/sync-3/arui-1/flows-1: the delete tombstone fuses 'the server still owes me a delete' (retryable, bounded, not user-facing) with 'do not resurrect this id' (durable, revocable only by explicit re-acquisition). One principle closes all three: a verdict may be revoked only by the authority that issued it or by the disappearance of the condition that produced it — never by the client's intention to try again. Add a separate transient `retryingIDs` for in-flight retries and the tension between flows-2 and sync-4 dissolves.

FOUR REVIEWERS INDEPENDENTLY FOUND THE SAME DELETE-TOMBSTONE DEFECT (sync-3, concurrency-1, arui-1, flows-1) AND THREE FOUND THE SAME UNGUARDED AWAIT AT DropStore.swift:281 (concurrency-4, arui-5, flows-6). Convergence at that rate is not redundancy, it is a signal about where the code resists reasoning. Both sites share a shape: an invariant asserted in a doc comment (:196-198 're-checks it after every await'; :492-496 'the tombstone stays') and enforced only by reviewer attention. Both fixes should therefore be structural, not local — a single generation-checked publish helper that makes a bare post-await assignment impossible, and a two-set tombstone model that makes an unretirable in-flight state unrepresentable.

PREDICATES THAT PROVE NOTHING ARE GUARDING DESTRUCTIVE OPERATIONS. The orphan reap at :321 destroys the user's durable outbox and is gated on `localReadWarning == nil` — a user-facing STRING. That string is nil after an absent-file load, and (the trigger no reviewer identified) it is also nil after a quarantine whose best-effort `try? writeIncident` failed, which is exactly what happens on the full disk that caused the corruption. Meanwhile the same string is non-nil forever after any transient read failure on an empty library, which disables the reap in the opposite direction. One string is simultaneously too permissive and too restrictive for a data-destroying gate. The fix is a returned sum type — `LoadOutcome { clean(rowCount:), skippedRows, quarantined, absent, unreadable }` — that cannot be forged by a failed side-channel write. Related: `try?` on the journal write is the wrong error policy for the one record whose entire purpose is surviving the failure that produced it.

THE SECURITY RULES ARE NOT IN THE REPOSITORY. web/firebase.json declares hosting only — no firestore block, no firestore.rules, no emulator config, no rules tests. Yet four findings turn entirely on rules semantics (whether a delete of a nonexistent doc returns permission-denied or not-found), FirebaseDropStore.swift:90-97 hardcodes one answer, and no test in the suite can assert it. The premise is correct — under owner-gated rules `resource` is null for an absent document, so the condition errors and Firestore returns PERMISSION_DENIED — but the codebase cannot demonstrate that, which is why a dead-code error mapping survived a full review round. Industrial standard: rules committed as code alongside the app, deployed from the same pipeline, and covered by @firebase/rules-unit-testing against the emulator with one test per error code the client maps. Until then every error-mapping decision in FirebaseDropStore is folklore.

SHARED LAST-WRITER-WINS SLOTS WERE EVICTED FROM DropLibrary AND REAPPEARED IN TWO OTHER FILES IN THE SAME ROUND. GeoARSessionManager.persistErrorText now carries asset-decode news (:1519), slider-persist failures (:1640, :1813) and received-drop save failures (RootView.swift:65) in one String with a 4 s auto-clear that any writer can reset — and the cosmetic writer fires from a per-frame factory, so it reliably evicts the data-loss writer. ReactionSession.delivery is a single slot with no per-send token while DropStore three files away implements exactly that token discipline. The eviction was applied to one class, not adopted as a rule. Make it one: any published state written from more than one call site needs an identity (which event), a severity (may it evict?) and a coalescing policy (what does a repeat do?) — the same three properties iOS requires of every UNNotificationRequest.

UI PRECEDENCE IS ENCODED AS AN if/else CHAIN IN A VIEW BUILDER. ProfileScreen.swift:74-113 determines what the user believes about their data through the ordering of SwiftUI branches, which is why 'Finishing N deletions…' can permanently occlude 'Synced' and why terminal correctly outranks pending only by accident of line order. Precedence over sync state is domain logic with a testable specification; it belongs on DropLibrary as a computed `enum SyncStatus` with an explicit order and unit tests, leaving the view to render. Concretely, deletions should not be in the ladder at all — the user considers a deleted drop deleted, and blocking a positive status on background cleanup they cannot act on is what converts a retry bug into a permanent product defect.

TESTS WERE WRITTEN THAT ASSERT THE BUG. Two round-4 tests actively defend defects: testPendingIDForAnUnloadableDropDoesNotStayUploadingForever (DropStoreTests.swift:397-410) refreshes over a URL that was never written and asserts the outbox was reaped — encoding 'the absence of a file proves the drops are gone'. testFailingLocalReadNeitherHidesTheFailureNorClearsState (:352-368) uses FlakyLocalStore, which is not a LocalDropStore, so the `as? LocalDropStore` downcast fails and the entire awaited branch it claims to cover never executes; it asserts only the hardcoded fallback string. This is worse than missing coverage — it converts open defects into closed ones in the review record. Root cause is the same in both: production branches keyed on a concrete type are unreachable from test doubles. Replace the downcasts with a protocol seam and both tests become expressible. Also note the suite has zero ReactionSession coverage, which is where the round's only CRITICAL regression lives.

THE DEVICE-MIGRATION PATH IS A SYSTEMATIC, UNHANDLED FAILURE AND ONLY sync-4 BRUSHES IT. Apple documents that everything in the app home directory except the bundle, Caches and tmp is backed up — so Library/Application Support/AugmentMeReality/drops.json restores to a new device with ownerUid values intact. Firebase iOS stores auth state in the keychain under a `...ThisDeviceOnly` accessibility class, and Apple documents that ThisDeviceOnly items do not migrate via backup. Therefore every iPhone upgrade deterministically yields: local rows owned by uid A, a fresh anonymous uid B, a cloud read (`whereField("ownerUid", isEqualTo: uid)`) that returns nothing, and every restored drop marked terminal-and-durable on its first edit or share, with the share sheet hard-refusing at ShareDropSheet.swift:184 and no reclaim UI anywhere. This is not an edge case; it is the modal upgrade path for the app's own users, and the codebase has no answer to it. Anonymous-account linking (Sign in with Apple) is the documented Firebase remedy and it preserves the uid; until that entitlement exists, a re-stamp-and-reupload affordance is mandatory.
research.shipVerdict: NOT PRODUCTION-GRADE FOR ITS CHARTER — but closer than the finding count suggests, and the gap is narrow and well-localised. WHAT ROUND 4 ACTUALLY ACHIEVED (and should not be relitigated): the sync-honesty redesign is genuinely good work. Per-drop state replaced shared last-writer-wins slots; one server-acknowledged write seam replaced three divergent copies; terminal failures became durable and outrank "Synced" in every surface; "Synced" became a computation over sets rather than a claim about a config file; the generation discipline in the write pipeline is correct and tested (testSupersededSyncTaskCannotClearPendingWhenItFinallyResumes is a real test of a real hazard). On the sync surfaces, failure is now visible. WHY IT STILL FAILS THE CHARTER: the round applied its own principle asymmetrically and, in one place, inverted it. Three residuals genuinely block. (1) THE PAYOFF LOOP IS GATED ON A SERVER ACCEPT (sync-1 / concurrency-2 / arui-2 / flows-3, plus flows-4's orphan-ack variant). startWrap is the only route into .memory anywhere in the app, and neither reactionFailed nor any timeout calls it — so offline, on a rules rejection, and on the notSignedIn fast-fail alike, the session strands in .watching with "Sending to Alex…" forever and the X button as the only exit. This is not "failure made visible"; it is failure made terminal, in the field condition an outdoor geo-drop app lives in. It is also a regression from round 3. (2) THE DELETE TOMBSTONE IS UNRETIRABLE AND SILENTLY DESTRUCTIVE (sync-3 / concurrency-1 / arui-1 / flows-1). "Synced" becomes unreachable for the life of the install after one ordinary offline-create-then-delete, and — the part that makes it a blocker rather than a cosmetic defect — the whole-merged-set suppression at DropStore.swift:314 silently deletes a legitimately re-received drop from every screen while its row survives on disk, unreachable and undeletable. That is silent data loss produced by the failure-visibility machinery itself. (3) THE DEVICE-MIGRATION DEAD END (sync-4 + flows-2). Application Support is backed up; Firebase's keychain auth state is ThisDeviceOnly and is not. Every iPhone upgrade therefore marks the user's restored drops terminal, durably, with the reporting surface hard-refusing the retry that would clear it — while flows-2's enqueue-time clearTerminal simultaneously lets an offline slider nudge erase the verdict and hand out a dead link. One mechanism cannot be escaped and the other cannot be trusted. NOT BLOCKING, fix in the same pass: concurrency-3 (profile clobber — real, HIGH, but user-recoverable by re-editing); the :281 unguarded await (concurrency-4 / arui-5 / flows-6 — bounded by the next refresh); the incident-journal deadlock (sync-2 / concurrency-5 — persists only until the user creates another drop); the banner layering (sync-5); the makeHolder announcements (sync-6 / concurrency-6 / arui-6); flows-5's unreaped terminal ids and the missing padding condition. SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE NEXT ACTION: rewrite FirestoreAcked as a bounded, cancellable, three-valued seam — one file, roughly thirty lines. Wrap the continuation in withTaskCancellationHandler, race it against Task.sleep in a withThrowingTaskGroup, and return `enum WriteOutcome { case acked, queuedLocally, rejected(Error) }` instead of Void-or-throw. That one change is upstream of nearly everything blocking: the reaction wrap becomes reachable because .queuedLocally starts it with honest copy ("Will send when you're back online" — which is true, Firestore's local write queue survives app restarts); syncTasks[id]?.cancel() and deleteTasks stop leaking permanently-parked continuations and stop silently blocking reconcileCloud retries; the delete retry budget actually spends; flows-2's offline trap gains an outcome to react to; and every UI surface gains the missing third state that the current binary success/throw model forced the round to fake by gating lifecycles on acks. Do that first, then the reaction-session token (concurrency-2/flows-4) and the two-set tombstone split become small, local, testable changes rather than redesigns. Sequence after that: tombstone split + never-acked short-circuit → terminal revalidation on auth-ready + delete the :442 clearTerminal → seedProfile single-flight with create-only rules → the LoadOutcome sum type (which closes arui-3, sync-2, concurrency-5 and the :281 double-await together) → UI polish. One process item worth insisting on before the next round: commit firestore.rules with emulator-backed rules tests. Four of this review's findings turn on rules behavior the repository cannot assert, and that is precisely how a dead error-code mapping survived a full round of review.
